build.title: Take-home pay, line by line
build.answers: How much of my pay actually reaches my account?
build.intro: Answers one question: once every line on the payslip comes off, what reaches your account?

inputs.label: First figure on the payslip. The label is set per edition in regions.ts: 'Monthly CTC' (India), 'Gross pay this month' (Europe), 'Gross pay on this paycheck' (US)
inputs.hint: The top figure on the offer letter, contract or pay stub, before anything comes off. India: if your CTC counts gratuity or a yearly bonus, take them off first. They are in the CTC but not in monthly pay.
inputs.source: example: the payslips in in/money-basics/first-payslip, eu/money-basics/first-payslip and us/money-basics/first-paycheck

inputs.label: Basic pay, % of CTC
inputs.hint: Both provident fund shares are 12% of basic pay. The salary breakup on your offer shows your basic; half of CTC is this example's figure.
inputs.source: example (the lesson's ₹17,500 basic on ₹35,000); the 12% rule: https://newsonair.gov.in/central-govt-notifies-employees-provident-fund-scheme-2026/

inputs.label: Professional tax this month
inputs.hint: A state tax. Some states charge none, and the Constitution caps it at ₹2,500 a year. ₹200 is an example.

inputs.label: TDS this month (copy it from your payslip)
inputs.hint: Income tax taken month by month. This tool never works it out. On the lesson's payslip it is ₹0.

inputs.label: Pension contribution (the amount on your payslip)
inputs.hint: The tool prints the rate this comes to, 9% here. Each country sets its own rate.

inputs.label: Health cover (the amount on your payslip)
inputs.hint: Your share of public health cover, as printed.

inputs.label: Unemployment cover (the amount on your payslip)
inputs.hint: Your share of support if you lose a job later, as printed.

inputs.label: Income tax this month (the amount on your payslip)
inputs.hint: The employer's monthly estimate of your year's tax, sent on to the tax authority. Copy it; the tool never works it out.

inputs.label: Employer contributions, if your payslip prints them
inputs.hint: Paid by the employer on top of gross pay. Shown beside the ledger, never taken off your pay.

inputs.label: Hours on this paycheck
inputs.hint: Check them against your own note of the shifts you worked.

inputs.label: Hourly rate
inputs.hint: Hours times the rate should equal the gross pay line. If not, the tool says by how much.

inputs.label: Federal income tax withheld (copy it from your stub)
inputs.hint: Set by your W-4. $110 is this stub's figure.

inputs.label: State income tax withheld (copy it from your stub)
inputs.hint: Depends on your state, and some states have none. Type 0 then.

inputs.label: How often you are paid (a select: weekly, every two weeks, twice a month, monthly)
inputs.hint: Every two weeks means 26 paychecks a year. Most months hold two and two months hold three.

outputs: Headline (Figure): what reaches your account. India ₹30,600, 'In-hand pay a month'. Europe €1,150, 'Net pay this month'. US $1,317.60, 'Net pay on this paycheck'.

Ledger, India: Monthly CTC ₹35,000; − Employer's EPF share (12% of the ₹17,500 basic) ₹2,100; = Gross salary ₹32,900; − Your EPF share ₹2,100; − Professional tax ₹200; − TDS ₹0; double-ruled In-hand pay ₹30,600.

Ledger, Europe: Gross pay €1,500; − Pension contribution, 9.0% of gross, €135; − Health cover, 9.0%, €135; − Unemployment cover, 2.0%, €30; − Income tax, 3.3%, €50; double-ruled Net pay €1,150. Each label prints the rate its typed amount comes to.

Ledger, US: a check row first, '80 hours × $20 = $1,600.00, matches the gross line' (or 'differs by $X: check the hours and the rate against the stub'); then Gross pay $1,600.00; − Social Security, 6.2%, $99.20; − Medicare, 1.45%, $23.20; − Federal income tax $110.00; − State income tax $50.00; double-ruled Net pay $1,317.60.
Fact: share of the first figure that arrives: 87.4% of the CTC, 76.7% of gross, 82.4% of gross.

Fact, India: held in your provident fund and pension scheme each month, both shares together, ₹4,200. Europe: your employer pays €300 on top, so the job costs it €1,800. US: your employer pays the same $122.40 again.
Fact, US: at 26 paychecks a year, $34,257.60. Most months hold two paychecks ($2,635.20), and two months a year hold three.

A 'Rules as of' line under the result, each rule with its source link and date: India, EPF 12% of basic (EPF Scheme 2026) and the ₹25,000 wage ceiling (17 Sep 2026); US, Social Security 6.2% and Medicare 1.45% (IRS Topic 751).
A link under the result, 'Plan the month in the budget planner', to budget#income={in-hand pay; net pay; for the US, the usual two-paycheck month}. The figure goes after the #.
build.resultSentence: Of {startLabel} of {start}, {net} reaches your account: {netShare}% of it. {deducted} comes off in {lineCount} lines{India: , and {fundTotal} of that is held in your provident fund and pension scheme in your name}{US: . At {paydaysPerYear} paychecks a year that is {year}, and most months hold {usualCount}, {usualMonth}}. Example (India): Of a monthly CTC of ₹35,000, ₹30,600 reaches your account: 87.4% of it. ₹4,400 comes off in three lines, and ₹4,200 of that is held in your provident fund and pension scheme in your name.
build.maths: New in src/lib/finance.ts: takeHomeLines(input: TakeHomeInput): { start: number; lines: DeductionLine[]; fundTotal?: number; impliedPercents?: number[]; employerCost?: number; hoursCheck?: number; employerMatch?: number }, then the existing deductions(start, lines). Mode 'ctc' (India): basic = round2(start × basicPercent / 100); epf = round2(basic × epfRule.value / 100), with epfRule.value = 12 from regions.ts. lines = [{ label: "Employer's EPF share", amount: epf, subtotalLabel: 'Gross salary' }, { label: 'Your EPF share', amount: epf }, { label: 'Professional tax', amount: professionalTax }, { label: 'TDS', amount: tds }]. fundTotal = 2 × epf. Mode 'typed' (Europe): lines are the four typed amounts in payslip order. impliedPercents[i] = round1(amount_i / start × 100) when start > 0. employerCost = start + employerOnTop, a fact outside the chain. Mode 'fica' (US): ss = round2(start × 6.2 / 100) and medicare = round2(start × 1.45 / 100), both rates from regions.ts Rules. lines = [ss, medicare, federal, state]. hoursCheck = round2(hours × hourlyRate − start) when hours > 0 and hourlyRate > 0 (0 means the lines match). employerMatch = ss + medicare. The stub's gross, never hours × rate, drives the sum. perMonth(perPay, n ∈ {52, 26, 24, 12}): { year: round2(perPay × n), usualCount: floor(n / 12), usualMonth: round2(perPay × floor(n / 12)), monthsWithExtra: n − 12 × floor(n / 12) }. netShare = round1(net / start × 100). lineCount counts lines whose amount is above 0. Money is shown through exact(); percentages to 1 dp. Unit pins: India 35,000 / 50 / 200 / 0 gives running figures 32,900, 30,800, 30,600, 30,600, net 30,600, fund 4,200 and 87.4%. Europe 1,500 / 135 / 135 / 30 / 50 gives 1,150, implied 9.0, 9.0, 2.0 and 3.3, 76.7% and an employer cost of 1,800. US 1,600 / 110 / 50 gives ss 99.20, medicare 23.20, net 1,317.60, 82.4%, hoursCheck 0 and employerMatch 122.40. perMonth(1,317.60, 26) gives 34,257.60, 2 × 2,635.20 and 2 months with a third paycheck. A negative net is returned as it is, and the island words it.
edgeCases: Lines that add up to more than the first figure: no negative take-home is shown as an answer. The sentence reads 'These lines add up to more than the pay; check each one against the payslip', and the error text is tied to the last field.
First figure 0 or blank: the sentence asks for the top figure on the payslip instead of printing 0.
India: basic % below 0 or above 100 shows error text under the field, and the EPF lines drop to ₹0.

India: basic above the ₹25,000 wage ceiling (raised on 17 Sep 2026). A note says contributions above the ceiling depend on the employer's scheme, that this sum takes 12% of all of basic, and that your EPF line settles it. The pension/fund split of the employer's share is never shown, because it is unverified above the ₹15,000 pension wage ceiling.
India: professional tax above ₹208 a month. A note says some states charge more in one month to reach the ₹2,500 yearly cap.
US: hours or rate blank or 0. The check row is hidden, and the gross line drives the sum either way.
US: an exempt W-4, or a state with no income tax, is typed as 0.
US: Social Security stops at a yearly wage base far above one paycheck. How this is worked out says so and links IRS Topic 751 rather than printing the figure.
US: pre-tax 401(k) or health deductions are not modelled. How this is worked out says to subtract them as printed, and that the tool does not recompute withholding.
Europe: employer contributions are a fact outside the chain and never subtracted. A part-year or emergency-tax month is typed as printed.
No line computes income tax. TDS, federal, state and EU income tax are always copied from the payslip.
build.whyItHelps: CTC against in-hand pay is named 'a standard confusion' for first earners in India (docs/research/regional-core.md). The EU/OECD Financial Competence Framework lists reading a payslip in its 16–18 band, and REGIONAL_TEACHING names a payslip decoder as a format in all three editions. The research sweep found no gross-to-net decoder at Chase, Bank of America or NerdWallet. India's commercial 'CTC to in-hand' calculators either leave income tax out or end in filing and fund pitches. In the repo, DeductionExplorer runs this sum only inside lessons, and all three first-pay lessons name the budget planner, which starts from in-hand pay. LessonLayout also renders no tool link at all under a deduction explorable, so today these lessons send readers to no tool.
build.modelledOn: FDIC Money Smart's lettered pay statement (every line defined, works without JS), Wikifin's fictional student payslip, Jupiter's India line order (basic, PF, professional tax, TDS, net), and proposal 2's Europe design, where the reader types each amount and the tool prints the rate it comes to. What is different: nothing computes income tax, there is no pie chart, and no employer, insurer, salary account or filing funnel is named. It opens on the lesson's first payslip, not a mid-career adult.
risks: Stale rates (EPF 12%, the ₹25,000 ceiling, 6.2%, 1.45%): each is a Rule in regions.ts with a source and an asOf date, printed as 'Rules as of'. A unit test fails when any asOf is more than 12 months old (proposal 1's staleness test, added on both judges' advice).
Read as tax advice: the only computed lines are the fixed EPF and FICA shares. Proposal 2's 'nil up to ₹12,75,000' band is left out, because the content-legal judge ruled it a computed tax result.

Privacy, pay figures in a copied link: the link carries the numbers after the #, which browsers never send to a server (content-legal judge). A line beside the button says the link holds the figures on screen. No storage key is added, so /cookies is unchanged.
Europe flattened into four lines: the reader types amounts, not rates, so the tool fits every country and shows the reader their own rates. Every default is labelled an example.
The judges agreed on this tool. The typed-amount Europe design follows the engineering judge; the # links and the absence of any tax band follow the content-legal judge.

verify.lens: Skeptic, facts: every rate, threshold, cap and rule the spec relies on, checked against sources on 2026-09-22
problems: India: the '12% of basic' rule the tool is built on is out of date. The EPF Scheme 2026 (in force 29 Jun 2026) sets 12% of WAGES from each side, not 12% of basic (newsonair, 2 Jul 2026). Under the Code on Social Security 2020 s.2(88), wages are basic + DA + retaining allowance, and any excluded allowances above 50% of total pay are added back (Business Today, 11 Jul 2026; Labour Law Reporter). The 'Basic pay, % of CTC' input, its hint, the 'Rules as of: EPF 12% of basic' line and the ledger label '12% of the ₹17,500 basic' all state the old rule. A reader whose basic is under half their pay gets an EPF line that is too low.

India: the ₹25,000 ceiling is misdescribed. S.O. 5109(E) of 17 Sep 2026 is confirmed (newsonair; NatLawReview; inkl). The mandatory contribution stops at 12% of ₹25,000, which is ₹3,000 a side, and contributions above that are voluntary. Employers commonly cap them. The spec always takes 12% of all basic and only adds a note, so above the ceiling the default overstates both EPF lines and understates in-hand pay.

India: the tool cannot show a payslip with no EPF line. Chapter III coverage is mandatory only for establishments with 20 or more employees (Labour Law Reporter), which leaves out many first jobs. The only workaround is to type basic % = 0, which is wrong.

India: lines that low earners actually meet are missing. ESI (the employee share is on wages up to a monthly ceiling, commonly given as 0.75% up to ₹21,000; not confirmed on esic.gov.in) and state labour welfare fund deductions have no field. CTC items other than gratuity and bonus also have no field: the employer's ESI, EDLI and admin charges, and insurance. For a first earner on a ₹20,000 CTC, both Gross and In-hand will fail to match the payslip.

US: Social Security and Medicare are always computed as 6.2% and 1.45% of gross, which is wrong for readers in this age band. Students working for their own school pay no FICA (IRS 'Student exception to FICA tax', updated 28 Jun 2026). So do under-18s working in a parent's sole proprietorship (IRS 'Family employees', updated 10 Oct 2025). Section 125 pre-tax health deductions are not FICA wages (IRS cafeteria-plan FAQ, updated 27 Jun 2026), so a stub with such a deduction shows lower FICA than 7.65% of gross. The spec's 'subtract them as printed' advice then produces a net that does not match the stub.

US: there is no line for state or local payroll deductions beyond income tax. California SDI is 1.3% of all wages in 2026 (EDD, via search; not opened). Other states have disability or paid-leave lines, and some cities and school districts levy local income tax. In those places the double-ruled 'Net pay' will not match the stub.

Europe: four fixed labels (pension, health, unemployment, income tax) do not fit real payslips, contrary to the spec's claim that 'the tool fits every country'. Germany prints a separate long-term care insurance line: 1.8% employee share, plus 0.6% for childless employees over 23 (TK, 2026). It also prints church tax and the solidarity surcharge where they apply. The EU lesson's own video uses Ireland, whose payslip is PAYE, USC and PRSI: one combined social-insurance line and a second tax. None of these maps onto the four boxes.

US hours check: it tests hours × rate against gross. Under the FLSA, hours over 40 in a workweek are paid at no less than time and a half (DOL WHD). Any teen shift worker with overtime, tips or a shift differential would be told the stub 'differs by $X: check the hours and the rate', which reads like an error when there is none.

US paycheck count: 'Two months a year hold three' and 'at 26 paychecks a year' are stated as fixed. Some years have 27 biweekly or 53 weekly paydays, and the yearly figure assumes every paycheck equals this one, which a partial first paycheck breaks. Neither caveat is in the spec.

Rules line: it cites US Social Security 6.2% and Medicare 1.45% (confirmed, IRS Topic 751, updated 20 Jan 2026; 2026 wage base $184,500). It does not mention the 0.9% Additional Medicare Tax on wages over $200,000, which Topic 751 also sets. That is minor for this audience, but 'How this is worked out' names the wage base and skips this.

whyItHelps is factually wrong on one point. NerdWallet does offer a gross-to-take-home estimator: its Income Calculator / Net Income Estimation 'estimates how your gross income breaks down into taxes, deductions, and take-home pay' (NerdWallet Help Center). The claim 'found no gross-to-net decoder at... NerdWallet' should not ship.

Budget link as specified will not work. The spec links to budget#income=..., but tool-kit.tsx reads only window.location.search (line 27), and ToolActions writes url.search (line 153). The budget planner will ignore the hash. Switching every tool to hash links without a fallback would also break the existing ?query links.

Confirmed and fine: Article 276(2) caps professional tax at ₹2,500 a year, so the ₹208-a-month note is correct. The India lesson figures (35,000 → 32,900 → 30,800 → 30,600), the EU example (1,500 → 1,150; employer cost 1,800) and the US arithmetic (99.20 + 23.20; net 1,317.60; 26 × 1,317.60 = 34,257.60) are internally correct. LessonLayout does render DeductionExplorer with no toolHref, as the spec says.
fixes: India: replace input `basicPercent` with `pfWages`, an amount. Label: 'PF wages a month: basic pay plus dearness allowance, from your salary breakup'. Default in: '17500'. Hint: 'EPF is 12% of wages: basic plus DA. If allowances such as HRA and special allowance are more than half your pay, the excess counts as wages too.' Source: the EPF Scheme 2026 (newsonair, 2 Jul 2026) and Code on Social Security 2020 s.2(88). Maths: epfBase = pfWages. Add an edge case: when pfWages is less than half of Gross, a note says 'Under the labour codes allowances above half your pay count as wages, so your EPF line may be higher than this; your payslip settles it.' Do not compute the add-back. Change the ledger label to "Employer's EPF share (12% of ₹17,500 PF wages)" and the Rules line to 'EPF 12% of wages (EPF Scheme 2026, from 29 Jun 2026)'.

India: add a select `pfOn` with three options: 'all PF wages' (default), 'wages up to the ₹25,000 ceiling' and 'no EPF on this payslip'. Maths: epf = pfOn === 'none' ? 0 : round2(min(pfWages, pfOn === 'capped' ? epfRule.ceiling : Infinity) × epfRule.value / 100), with epfRule = { value: 12, ceiling: 25000, asOf: '2026-09-17', source: S.O. 5109(E), newsonair }. Rewrite the above-ceiling note: 'The compulsory share stops at 12% of ₹25,000, ₹3,000 a side; above that it is voluntary and many employers cap it. Pick what your payslip shows.' The hint for 'none': 'Employers with fewer than 20 staff need not enrol you.' Add a unit pin: pfWages 30,000 capped gives epf 3,000.

India: add two typed fields, each defaulting to 0 and copied as printed. `otherEmployerCosts`: "Other employer costs counted in the CTC (employer's ESI, gratuity, insurance, EDLI/admin charges)", subtracted before the Gross salary subtotal. `otherDeductions`: 'ESI, labour welfare fund or any other line on your payslip', subtracted after professional tax. The ESI hint says only 'At lower pay an ESI line appears; copy it as printed'. Do not print 0.75% or ₹21,000 until they are confirmed on esic.gov.in and entered as a Rule with asOf. Pins stay unchanged at 0.

US: stop computing FICA. Make `socialSecurity` (default '99.20') and `medicare` (default '23.20') typed-as-printed inputs, like Europe's lines. Keep 6.2% and 1.45% as Rules (IRS Topic 751, asOf 2026-01-20) and use them only in a check row: 'Social Security is 6.2% of $1,600 = $99.20: matches.' Otherwise: 'differs by $X: a pre-tax health plan lowers the pay these are worked on; students working for their own school, and under-18s working in a parent's business, pay none. Check the stub.' Sources: IRS student-exception page, IRS family-employees page, IRS cafeteria-plan FAQ. employerMatch = typed socialSecurity + medicare. Pins are unchanged at the defaults: net 1,317.60, 82.4%, employerMatch 122.40.

It becomes one ledger line before Net pay. Change the pre-tax 401(k)/health edge case to say that these are typed here and that FICA is copied from the stub, so the tool never recomputes a lowered wage base.

Europe: replace the four fixed inputs with reader-labelled rows (label + amount, up to 8), on the budget planner's row pattern. Prefill them with the lesson's four example rows. Each row prints 'comes to X.X% of gross'. Hint: 'Name each line as your payslip does: long-term care insurance, church tax, PRSI, USC. Countries print different lines.' Replace 'the tool fits every country' in risks with 'the reader copies each printed line, so any country's payslip can be entered'. Cite TK 2026 for the German care-insurance example if the hint names a rate.

The mismatch wording becomes 'differs by $X: tips, a shift premium or a pay error can explain it; check the hours lines on the stub'. Source: dol.gov/agencies/whd/overtime. Add a unit pin: 80 h + 4 OT at $20 against a gross of $1,720 gives hoursCheck 0.

How this is worked out, US: after the Social Security wage-base sentence, add 'Medicare has no cap, and an extra 0.9% applies to wages over $200,000 in a year (IRS Topic 751)'. Keep the link rather than printing the base.

verify.lens: safety-and-scope skeptic: advice, recommendation, product naming, promised returns, personal data, moralising, content rules, and maths edge cases (zero, negative, huge, non-integer, rounding, select values, links)
problems: P1 (wrong headline figure). Each edition has a fixed set of lines, so many real payslips cannot be entered and the in-hand or net figure comes out too high, with no way to match it to the stub. India has no ESI line. ESI takes 0.75% from employees whose gross is at or below ₹21,000 a month, which is exactly the first-job pay range. Europe's four labels have no place for care insurance or church tax, and Ireland's PRSI and USC (the country in the lesson's own video) do not fit 'pension, health, unemployment'. The US has no place for state disability or paid-leave deductions (California, New York, New Jersey, Washington and others), local income tax, or pre-tax benefits. The edge case 'subtract them as printed' refers to a field that does not exist.

P2 (India EPF computed with no override). EPF is always 12% of all basic, and the reader cannot correct it. That is wrong in four common cases. (a) Employers who cap contributions at the wage ceiling: the spec only adds a note, and the headline figure stays wrong. (b) Since 21 Nov 2025, under the Labour Codes, if excluded allowances are more than 50% of pay, the excess counts as wages, so a basic % below 50 under-computes PF. (c) Establishments with fewer than 20 employees, and apprentices or trainees, often have no EPF at all. (d) Voluntary PF. On top of that, 'Basic pay, % of CTC' asks the reader to work out a percentage that neither the payslip nor the offer prints. The only start point is 'Monthly CTC', which is an offer-letter figure: most Indian payslips begin at gross earnings. round2 also produces paise, such as ₹2,100.48 on a ₹17,504 basic, where payslips print whole rupees.

P3 (US FICA always computed). Social Security and Medicare are forced to 6.2% and 1.45% of gross. That gives the wrong net pay for: students employed by their own school or college (the IRS student FICA exception); F-1 and J-1 nonresident students in their first five years (exempt, per IRS); under-18s employed by a parent's sole proprietorship; anyone with Section 125 pre-tax health premiums (a lower FICA wage base); and very large inputs above the $184,500 wage base for 2026 or the $200,000 Additional Medicare threshold. The tool would print FICA lines the reader's stub does not have, and they could not correct them.

P4 (float rounding, verified in node). round2(start × rate / 100) rounds half-cents down because of binary floating point. Gross $150 gives Medicare $2.17 where payroll gives $2.18. $162.50 gives Social Security $10.07 where payroll gives $10.08. The same happens at $10, $70, $262.50 and $317.50. These are realistic teen paychecks, so the tool would disagree with a correct stub by a cent.

P5 (hours check flags lawful pay as an error). The 'differs by $X: check the hours and the rate' message fires on legitimate differences: overtime at 1.5 times when one week of the two is over 40 hours, tips for tipped workers, shift differentials, a second rate, or a bonus. It also fires on sub-cent payroll rounding: 37.5 h × $15.35 = $575.625, which a stub prints as $575.62, gives 'differs by $0.01'. It implies the employer made a mistake when none was made.

P6 (pay-frequency wording and projection). The template 'most months hold {usualCount} … two months a year hold three' is wrong for twice a month (n=24: every month holds 2) and monthly (n=12: every month holds 1). It also ignores years with 27 biweekly or 53 weekly paydays. The yearly figure ($34,257.60) and the budget hand-off ($2,635.20) assume every paycheck equals this one, which is an unlabelled projection for readers with variable shifts or a summer-only job. paidEvery arriving from a link is not checked against the four allowed values, so n can be undefined and the result NaN.

P7 (input validation gaps). A negative first figure is not handled; only 0 or blank is. Negative typed amounts are not handled either, whether a typo or a real refund line such as an Irish PAYE refund. A blank basic % silently becomes EPF ₹0. The 'lines exceed pay' error is tied to 'the last field', which is a select in the US, and in India the EPF lines are computed rather than typed. The spec does not say that the Figure, the facts, the yearly projection and the budget link are all withheld when net ≤ 0.

P8 (misleading fact on blank input). In Europe, employerOnTop blank or 0 prints 'your employer pays €0 on top, so the job costs it €1,500'. That reads as a factual claim that the employer pays nothing, when the payslip simply did not print the line.

P9 (inaccurate wording). 'held in your provident fund and pension scheme in your name' is wrong for the pension part. The share of the employer's contribution that goes to the pension scheme (EPS) is a pension entitlement, not a balance held in the reader's name. The lesson itself says only that part of the employer's share 'funds the pension scheme'.

P10 (percent display disagrees with the unit pin). netShare = round1(…) pins 82.4% for the US. The site's existing percent() formatter applied to the raw fraction 1317.6/1600 prints 82.3% (checked in node). If the island formats the fraction, the unit test and the screen will disagree.

P11 (mixed decimals in one ledger). exact() prints integers with no decimals and others with 2, so the US ledger would show '$1,600' next to '$99.20' and '$110' next to '$23.20'. The spec's own outputs show '$1,600.00' and '$110.00'.

P12 (# links break existing links). tool-kit readQuery and BudgetPlanner both read only window.location.search. SplitExplorer hands off to the planner with ?income=&rows=, and the e2e tests pin ?-style links. Moving ToolActions to # without reading both would break every link already shared and the lesson-to-planner hand-off. Pay figures written to the address bar also sit in history, which matters on the shared phones REGIONAL_TEACHING documents (18%).

P13 (lesson linking gap). DeductionExplorer has no toolHref prop and LessonLayout passes none, so changing lesson frontmatter alone still gives the lessons no link to the tool. build.title: A loan's cost as a yearly rate
build.answers: I get this much and pay back that much: what is that as a yearly rate?
build.short: What is this loan as a yearly rate?
build.intro: Answers one question: whatever the charge is called, a fee, a flat rate or 'no-cost', what does it come to over a year?

inputs.label: Amount borrowed
inputs.hint: The loan amount on the offer, or the price of the thing bought on instalments.
inputs.source: example: in/protect-your-money/cost-of-borrowing ('₹500 to lend ₹5,000 for seven days')

inputs.label: Fees taken at the start
inputs.hint: Processing fees and any GST on them, taken before the money reaches you or paid on the day. The Key Facts Statement lists every charge. Interest taken up front counts here too.

inputs.label: Each repayment
inputs.hint: One payment, or each equal instalment. For a flat-rate offer, type the instalment printed on the offer.

inputs.label: Number of repayments
Days between repayments
inputs.hint: 7 for a week. 30 or 31 counts as a month, 12 to a year.

outputs: Headline (Figure): {nominal}% a year, labelled 'worked out from your figures' (default: 521.4%).
Ledger: Amount borrowed ₹5,000; − Fees taken at the start ₹0; = Reaches you ₹5,000; Repaid, 1 × ₹5,500, ₹5,500; double-ruled Cost of borrowing (repaid minus what reached you) ₹500.
Fact: rate for one period, 10% for each 7 days.
Fact: periods in a year, 52.1.
Fact: charged period after period it compounds to over 10,000% a year (the effective figure, capped in display).
Fact: 'The APR on a regulated lender's Key Facts Statement is the official figure. Set this beside it.'

How this is worked out: the charge divided by what reached you, times the periods in a year (the lesson's method); for instalments, the rate at which the repayments are worth what reached you; a warning about the flat-rate shortcut; a note that this is not the lender's own APR method.
build.resultSentence: Getting {received} and repaying {count} × {repayment} costs {cost}: {perPeriod}% for each {period}, which is {nominal}% a year. Example: Getting ₹5,000 and repaying 1 × ₹5,500 costs ₹500: 10% for each 7 days, which is 521.4% a year. (The phone plan in the lesson's quiz reads: Getting ₹11,400 and repaying 3 × ₹4,000 costs ₹600: 2.6% for each month, which is 31.3% a year.)
build.maths: yearlyRate(amount, fee, repayment, count, days): { received, repaid, cost, perPeriod, periodsPerYear, nominal, effective } | { error }. received = round2(amount − fee); repaid = round2(repayment × count); cost = round2(repaid − received). periodsPerYear = 12 when 28 ≤ days ≤ 31, otherwise 365 / days. perPeriod is 0 when repaid ≤ received, and exactly repaid / received − 1 when count is 1. Otherwise bisection solves received = repayment × (1 − (1 + i)^−count) / i on [0, hi]: hi starts at 1 and doubles while PV(hi) > received, then 200 iterations. nominal = perPeriod × periodsPerYear × 100, the rate for one period times the periods in a year, which is the lesson's method. effective = ((1 + perPeriod)^periodsPerYear − 1) × 100. Both display to 1 dp; an effective figure above 10,000 shows as 'over 10,000%'. Pins: 5,000 / 0 / 5,500 / 1 / 7 gives 10% a period, 52.14 periods and 521.4% (the lesson's 'about 521%'), effective over 10,000%. 12,000 / 600 / 4,000 / 3 / 30 (the lesson quiz's phone) gives 2.61% a month, 31.3% and 36.2%. 20,000 / 0 / 1,966.67 / 12 / 30 (18% flat over a year) gives 31.7% and 36.8%. 1,50,000 / 0 / 4,910.81 / 36 / 30 (first-business-loan's Key Facts Statement) gives 11.0%, effective 11.6%, cost 26,789.16. 10,000 / 0 / 10,000 / 1 / 30 gives 0.
edgeCases: Repaid equal to what reached you: 'It costs nothing extra: 0% a year.'
Repaid less than what reached you: error text asking to check the figures; no negative rate is shown.
Fees equal to or above the amount: 'Nothing reaches you', with no rate.
Amount, count or days of 0 or blank: error text under the field. A count that is not whole is rounded down, with a note.
Very high rates: the headline stays the nominal rate, and the effective fact shows 'over 10,000%'.
Days from 28 to 31 count as monthly; otherwise 365 / days, so a 91-day app loan fits.
Unequal instalments, a large last payment or grace months are not supported. How this is worked out says so and points to the Key Facts Statement's APR.
Late fees and bounce charges are left out, as in an APR, and How this is worked out says so.
Flat-rate offers: type the printed instalment. How this is worked out warns that the shortcut '2 × flat ÷ (1 + years)' in search snippets is wrong: 18% flat over a year is 31.7%, not 18%.
build.whyItHelps: The India lesson 'Every loan as a yearly rate' opens its first section with this sum (₹500 on ₹5,000 for seven days is about 521%), and its first quiz check is a 'no-cost' phone plan with a ₹600 fee. RBI has warned that unauthorised lending apps charge excessive rates and hidden charges, and its Digital Lending Directions 2025 make the APR on the Key Facts Statement the figure to compare. REGIONAL_TEACHING lists unregulated loan apps as a core India money situation. The research sweep found that India's APR tools start at 12 months (Axis Finance), that flat-vs-reducing tools answer 'save ₹X' instead of giving a rate, and that a wrong shortcut formula circulates in search snippets. The existing loan tool runs forward from a rate and cannot take a fee or a 7-day term.
build.modelledOn: Axis Finance's APR calculator, where a fee taken at the start raises the yearly cost, and the Key Facts Statement itself; Groww's flat-vs-reducing inputs. What is different: terms in days, so a 7-day or 91-day app loan fits; an exact, tested solve instead of a rule of thumb; no 'save ₹X' headline and no winner; no app name, logo or 'Apply now'.
risks: Mistaken for the lender's APR: labelled 'worked out from your figures' with the lesson's own method, and the Key Facts Statement APR is named as the official figure.
Sensational numbers: the headline is the nominal rate, and the compounded figure is a fact capped at 'over 10,000%'.
Making a loan look acceptable: the sentence states the cost and the rate only. It gives no verdict and compares no offers.

GST: the engineering judge asked for proposal 1's fee and GST rows; the content-legal judge flagged the 18% GST rate as unverified. Settled as one fee field in money ('and any GST on them', as the Key Facts Statement lists it) with no GST rate held: safety goes to the content-legal judge, the extra row to the engineering judge.
India only until the Europe (APRC, effective) and US (Reg Z) conventions are verified and a lesson in those editions teaches it (engineering judge's condition).

Negative, fractional and huge inputs are not handled. toNumber (tool-kit.tsx:18) keeps '-'. Days of -7 give periodsPerYear -52.1 and a headline of -521.4% a year. A fee of -500 pushes received above the amount. Days of 0.01 give 36,500 periods. The spec's edge cases cover only 0 or blank.

The headline has no cap: only the effective figure is capped. 5,000 / 4,999.99 / 5,500 / 1 / 7 puts 2,867,851,928.6% a year in the headline, which goes against the spec's own 'sensational numbers' risk. The bisection has no cap on how many times it doubles.

Rounding makes real zero-cost plans fail. A 'no-cost' ₹10,000 plan at 3 × ₹3,333.33 repays 9,999.99, which is less than received, so the reader gets the 'check the figures' error. 6 × ₹1,666.67 costs ₹0.02 and prints '0.0% a year' beside a nonzero cost. The maths text also contradicts itself: 'perPeriod is 0 when repaid ≤ received' against an error when repaid is less.

'It costs nothing extra: 0% a year' judges the whole offer from partial inputs. The tool leaves out tax added to each instalment, advance instalments and late fees, which is exactly the 'no-cost' trap the lesson's first quiz check teaches. It reads as reassurance.

The solve assumes the first repayment falls one period after the money arrives (RBI Annex B: 'Commencement of repayments 30 days'). The spec never says so and gives no way to enter an instalment paid on the day, which is common for goods bought on instalments. The lesson's phone (12,000 / 600 / 4,000 × 3) is 31.3% a year with the first part a month later, but 64.3% a year if the first part is paid on the day (12,000 / 4,600 / 4,000 / 2 / 30). That is double.

The label 'Days between repayments' is wrong for a single repayment, where it means the days until the repayment is due. The hint says '30 or 31 counts as a month', but the maths uses 28 to 31. A 28-day cycle counted as 12 a year rather than 13.04 understates the rate by 8%, the direction that flatters the loan.

The word 'effective' conflicts with the KFS, and the claim of a different method is wrong. The RBI KFS Annex B calls its APR the 'Effective annualized interest rate'. It computes it as the monthly IRR on the net disbursed amount × 12: ₹20,000, ₹400 fees, 24 × ₹969.73 gives 17.07%, which I checked; compounding gives 18.47%. That is exactly the spec's nominal method. Yet the spec calls the compounded figure 'the effective figure' and says the tool is 'not the lender's own APR method'. A reader holding a KFS would see 'Effective 17.07%' there and 'effective 18.5%' here. Also, showing 'over 10,000%' as a Fact on load for a one-off 7-day loan that is never compounded is a scare figure.

The spec states without a source that '2 × flat ÷ (1 + years)' circulates in search snippets. I could not find it. The common rules of thumb are multipliers of about 1.8 to 1.95, or 2n/(n+1) with n counted in instalments (about 33.2% for 18% flat over 12 instalments). The page would be asserting what third-party pages say with nothing to back it.

The fee hint says 'The Key Facts Statement lists every charge', and a Fact calls the KFS APR 'the official figure'. But the KFS circular exempts credit card receivables, so a card's instalment plan, the spec's 'price of the thing bought on instalments' case, has no KFS. The hint also leaves out third-party charges collected through the lender (insurance, legal charges). Annex B counts these in the APR: ₹160 of its ₹400.

The ledger does not reach the answer. It closes with a double rule under the rupee cost, but the question asks for a yearly rate, and the brand puts the double rule under the final answer. For instalments, the rate for each period comes from a hidden solve the reader cannot check (for example, 2.6% a month on the phone).
At load, the headline label 'worked out from your figures' describes the example's figures, not the reader's. The count-1 sentence reads 'repaying 1 × ₹5,500'.

verify.lens: skeptic: facts, rates and rules checked against sources, plus the maths pins and repo wiring
problems: WRONG CLAIM, lender's APR method: the spec's 'How this is worked out' says the tool is 'not the lender's own APR method'. RBI's own KFS illustration (Annex B, 15 Apr 2024) says APR is 'computed on net disbursed amount using IRR approach and reducing balance method'. Its worked case is sanctioned ₹20,000, fees ₹400, net disbursed ₹19,600, 24 monthly EMIs of ₹969.73 (printed ₹970), APR 17.07%. I reproduced it: the monthly IRR is 1.4225%, and 1.4225% × 12 = 17.070%. Compounded it would be 18.47%. So the spec's 'nominal' is the RBI method for equal monthly instalments with fees taken at the start. Telling readers otherwise would make them distrust a KFS APR that should match the tool.

CONFLICTING TERM 'effective': RBI's Annex B names the APR (the × 12 figure) the 'Effective annualized interest rate'. The spec uses 'effective' for the compounded figure (((1+i)^n − 1)), and the lesson details use 'effective APR' the same way, following the Khan video. A reader holding a KFS will match the wrong number. Example: the tool's 'effective' 18.5% against the KFS 'effective annualized' 17.07%.

WRONG GST HINT: footnote 4 of RBI's KFS template (Annex A) says lenders 'may disclose the amount net of any taxes such as GST'. The NBFC Responsible Business Conduct Directions 2025 carry the same rule. The fee hint ('Processing fees and any GST on them… The Key Facts Statement lists every charge') and the risk note ('as the Key Facts Statement lists it') are therefore wrong. A reader copying the KFS fee line can leave out the GST they actually pay. The sources do not say whether the KFS APR itself includes GST, so the spec must not imply it.

UNSTATED TIMING ASSUMPTION gives wrong answers: the solve assumes the first repayment falls one full period after the money arrives (an ordinary annuity). RBI's illustration shows 'Commencement of repayments, post sanction: 30 days', which fits. Shop instalment plans often take the first part on the day. The lesson quiz's phone (₹12,000, ₹600 fee, 3 × ₹4,000) gives 31.3% under the spec's assumption. With the first part paid on the day it is 64.3%, so the tool would show about half the true rate, with no warning.

DISCONTINUITY, and a hint that contradicts the maths: the maths counts 28–31 days as 12 periods, but the input hint says '30 or 31 counts as a month'. At the boundary, ₹500 on ₹5,000 over 27 days shows 135.2% a year. Over 28 days it shows 120.0%, where 365/28 would give 130.4%. Adding one day drops the rate by 15 points.

LEDGER ROUNDING DOES NOT ADD UP: the facts print 10% × 52.1 periods but the headline is 521.4% (10 × 52.1 = 521.0). They print 2.6% a month but the headline is 31.3% (2.6 × 12 = 31.2). BRAND_GUIDE §5 requires a ledger 'whose rows add up', and a reader checking by hand will find a mismatch.

SHORT LOANS CAN DIFFER FROM A LENDER'S APR: RBI does not fix the compounding unit for loans counted in days. On the 7-day case, a daily IRR × 365 gives 500.4%, while the spec's per-period × 365/7 gives 521.4%. 'Set this beside it' needs a caveat for day-based loans. The spec gives none.

POSSIBLY STALE SOURCE: the fee input cites the 15 April 2024 KFS circular (NotificationUser.aspx?Id=12663). On 28 Nov 2025 RBI withdrew 9,445 circulars into 244 entity-wise Master Directions. build.title: Card balance at the minimum payment
build.answers: If I pay only the minimum, how long does my card take to clear, and what does it cost?
build.short: How long does the minimum take?
build.intro: Answers one question: paying only the minimum, how many months until the balance is gone, and how much of what you pay is interest?

inputs.label: What you owe on the card
inputs.hint: The statement balance. The run assumes nothing new is spent on the card.
inputs.source: example: the statements in in/protect-your-money/cost-of-borrowing and us/money-basics/credit-file

inputs.label: Interest rate, % a year
inputs.hint: India: cards often print a monthly rate, and 3.5% a month is 42% a year; this one is an example. US: the purchase APR on your statement; 27.5% is the CFPB's average for new general-purpose cards opened in 2024, used as an example.

inputs.label: India: 'Minimum due, % of what you owe'. US: 'Minimum: the month's interest plus this % of the balance'. The label and the rule type are set per edition in regions.ts
inputs.hint: Each card's agreement sets the rule. This one is an example.
inputs.source: India: https://www.rbi.org.in/Scripts/BS_ViewMasDirections.aspx?id=12300 (the minimum must not let the balance grow), with 5% the lesson's example; US: example

inputs.label: Smallest minimum
inputs.hint: The minimum never drops below this until the last payment.
inputs.source: India: example; US: the $25 minimum on the lesson's $400 statement

inputs.label: A fixed amount each month, to compare
inputs.hint: India: ₹1,000 is the first month's minimum, kept the same. US: an example.

outputs: Headline (Figure): months to clear at the minimum, with years and months. India 142 months (11 years 10 months); US 20 months (1 year 8 months).

Ledger, month one, the statement line by line. India: Owed now ₹20,000; + Interest for the month ₹700; − Minimum paid ₹1,000; double-ruled Owed next month ₹19,700 (the lesson's situation). US: Statement balance $400.00; − Minimum paid $25.00; = Carried $375.00; + Interest on what carried $8.59; double-ruled Next statement $383.59.
Ledger, the whole run at the minimum: Owed now; + Interest over {months} months; double-ruled Total paid. India ₹20,000 + ₹40,332.68 = ₹60,332.68. US $400 + $89.79 = $489.79.
Fact: at a fixed {compare} a month. India ₹1,000: 35 months, ₹14,997.77 of interest. US $50: 9 months, $35.97.
Fact: paid in full by the due date, the purchases on a statement usually carry no interest.
The yearly schedule of the minimum run in a details fold (paid, interest, owed at the end of each year), with a table, as LoanEmi does.
Assumption line: no new spending, fees, late charges or (India) GST on interest, and the rate stays the same.
build.resultSentence: Paying only the minimum clears {balance} in {months} months ({years} years {remMonths} months) and adds {interest} of interest, {total} in all. At a fixed {compare} a month it clears in {cMonths} months and adds {cInterest}. Example (India): Paying only the minimum clears ₹20,000 in 142 months (11 years 10 months) and adds ₹40,332.68 of interest, ₹60,332.68 in all. At a fixed ₹1,000 a month it clears in 35 months and adds ₹14,997.77.
build.maths: minimumRun({ balance, aprPercent, rule: 'percent' | 'interest-plus', minPercent, minFloor, interestBase: 'statement' | 'carried', fixed?: number, maxMonths = 1200 }): { months: number | null; reason?: 'never-falls' | 'over-100-years'; totalInterest; totalPaid; first: { payment; interest; principal?; carried?; next }; years: ScheduleYear[] }. r = aprPercent / 1200. Every money value is rounded to 2 dp at each step (round2), and the balance b is carried rounded; this settles the one-paisa difference the engineering judge found. 'statement' (India, as the lesson's statement: a partly paid balance is charged the month's interest in full): i = round2(b × r); due = round2(b + i); min = rule 'percent' ? round2(minPercent / 100 × b) : round2(i + minPercent / 100 × b); pay = round2(Math.min(fixed ?? Math.max(min, minFloor), due)); if pay ≤ i and pay < due, return months: null, 'never-falls'; b = round2(due − pay). 'carried' (US, as the lesson's statement: the first statement has no interest, and what carries after the payment is charged): min = rule 'percent' ? round2(minPercent / 100 × b) : round2(lastI + minPercent / 100 × b), with lastI = 0 in month one; pay = round2(Math.min(fixed ?? Math.max(min, minFloor), b)); carried = round2(b − pay); i = round2(carried × r); if carried > 0 and i ≥ pay, return null, 'never-falls'; b = round2(carried + i); lastI = i. Stop when b ≤ 0.004. More than maxMonths returns null, 'over-100-years'. Years are 12-month blocks, as in amortization(). Pins: India 20,000 / 42 / percent 5 / 200 / statement gives 142 months, interest 40,332.68, paid 60,332.68, first 1,000 = 700 + 300 and next 19,700. Fixed 1,000 gives 35 months and 14,997.77. minPercent 3.5 or 3 gives null, never-falls. APR 0 gives 52 months with no interest. US 400 / 27.5 / interest-plus 1 / 25 / carried gives 20 months, interest 89.79 and paid 489.79; its first payment of 25 leaves 375.00 carried, 8.59 of interest and a next statement of 383.59. Fixed 50 gives 9 months and 35.97.
edgeCases: A minimum that does not cover the month's interest (India's rule at 3% with 42% a year): no months figure. The sentence says the balance never falls on this rule, that RBI's card directions require the minimum to be set so this cannot happen, and to check the rule on the statement.
A compare amount below the first minimum: 'Below the minimum due, so it would not count as on time', and the compare fact is hidden.
Balance at or below the floor: cleared in one payment.
APR 0: no interest line, and months come from the minimum alone.
More than 1,200 months: 'more than 100 years'.

New purchases, annual fees, late fees and India's GST on card interest are left out, and the assumption line says so. GST stays out until a dated official source is added; the lesson's ₹19,700 leaves it out too.
Blank or negative fields: error text under the field.
US grace period: How this is worked out says that paying in full by the due date usually means no interest on purchases (CFPB grace-period page, already a credit-file source).
build.whyItHelps: The India lesson opens on this statement (₹1,000 paid, only ₹300 less owed), and its document line reads 'Months or years to clear'. The US credit-file lesson's first check is the choice between the $25 minimum and the $400 balance. RBI's card directions and US Regulation Z both require a minimum-payment warning on statements, but neither warning uses the reader's own numbers. A run of minimum payments is a month-by-month loop that no lesson explorer can show. The research sweep found that Bankrate's minimum-payment calculator and Khan Academy's warning table teach it well, while the Indian versions sit beside card-to-cash services or use alarm wording.
build.modelledOn: Bankrate's minimum payment calculator (the rule as an input, the minimum against a fixed payment, the schedule behind a fold); Khan Academy's statement warning table; proposal 1's month-one statement ledger. What is different: the rule and floor are labelled examples, the order of interest and payment matches each edition's lesson, and there is no bank dropdown, card name, balance-transfer promotion or alarm wording.
risks: Minimum rules differ by card: rule, floor and rate are labelled example inputs, and the statement's own warning is named as the real figure.
Fear framing: the sentence states months and money flatly, and the 'paid in full: no interest on purchases' fact is always shown (content-legal judge).
Advice: it never says 'pay more' or 'get a different card', and the compare amount is the reader's own.
Accuracy: rounding is fixed at every step, and unit tests pin all four default runs (engineering judge).

US default corrected to the lesson's $400 balance and $25 minimum; the proposal's $1,000 is the card's limit (content-legal judge). With a $25 floor the US minimum never moves, so 'keep the first payment the same' would repeat the minimum run. The comparison is therefore a fixed-amount input.

problems: MATHS BUG (US, carried + interest-plus): the never-falls test `if carried > 0 and i >= pay` fires in month one because lastI = 0 then. It compares next month's interest with a minimum that has no interest in it yet. Re-run in node with the spec's exact algorithm: every US balance of $1,116 or more at the default 27.5% returns months: null, 'never-falls'. So $1,200, $2,000 and $5,000 would all tell a reader the balance never falls, and the sentence for that case cites RBI. The correct results are 89 months at $1,116, 147 months at $2,000 and 236 months at $5,000. The default $400 run hides the bug. CFPB puts the average balance at about $5,300, so real inputs will hit it.

COMPARE CHECK TOO NARROW: the edge case 'A compare amount below the first minimum' only checks month one. Under the US interest-plus rule, month two's minimum is higher than month one's once interest is added. Example: $1,000 with a fixed $30 passes month one (minimum $25) but is below the $32.15 minimum from month two. The page would show the compare fact for a payment that would be late.

STALE SOURCE: the spec cites the RBI Master Direction on credit and debit cards, 2022 (BS_ViewMasDirections id=12300, updated 7 March 2024). For commercial banks it was repealed and replaced by the Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Credit Cards and Debit Cards: Issuance and Conduct) Directions, 2025, dated 28 November 2025 (id=13155; repeal in para 93). The same rules sit in the new text: 23(2) no negative amortisation from the minimum amount due, and 23(3) the minimum-payment legend. The cost-of-borrowing lesson cites the old MD too.

FALSE CLAIM in whyItHelps: 'neither warning uses the reader's own numbers'. For the US this is wrong. Regulation Z §1026.7(b)(12) requires every statement to show the months to repay at the minimum, the total cost, and the 36-month payment and total, all worked from 'the current outstanding balance shown on the periodic statement'. Only India's RBI legend is a generic sentence.

US MODEL WILL NOT MATCH THE 'REAL FIGURE' IT POINTS TO: the risks line says the statement's own warning is the real figure. That box is worked under Reg Z Appendix M1 assumptions: no grace period (b)(4)(iv), and payments credited on the last day of the cycle (b)(4)(viii). The spec's 'carried' model charges interest only on what is left after the payment, so it will always show fewer months and less interest than the reader's own statement box. On the same $400 run, working interest on the whole balance gives 21 months and $104.02, against the spec's 20 months and $89.79. The spec never tells the reader why the figures differ.

INDIA INTEREST MODEL PRESENTED AS FACT, AGAINST RBI TEXT: the maths note says a partly paid balance is 'charged the month's interest in full'. RBI 2025 Directions para 23(6) (23(6) in the 2022 MD too) says 'Interest shall be levied only on the outstanding amount, adjusted for payments / refunds / reversed transactions'. Real cards work interest out day by day from each purchase date once a balance carries. The ₹700 = 3.5% × ₹20,000 figure is fine as the lesson's simplification, but the tool must not describe it as how Indian cards charge interest.

EDGE CASE CONTRADICTS THE PAGE'S OWN FACT: 'Balance at or below the floor: cleared in one payment' still charges interest in India's statement mode. A ₹150 balance pays ₹155.25, with ₹5.25 of interest. The same page always shows 'paid in full by the due date, the purchases on a statement usually carry no interest'.

NEVER-FALLS COPY IS INDIA-ONLY: the edge-case sentence cites RBI's card directions, but the same code path can fire in the US (fixed compare below interest, or the bug above). The US has no RBI rule, so the US needs its own wording.

US RULE AND FLOOR ARE MARKED 'example' WITH NO SOURCE, THOUGH ONE EXISTS: the same CFPB 2025 report (p.70) says most issuers set the minimum at 1% of the balance plus finance charges and fees. It also says the floors in 2025 agreements ran from $15 to $50, most often $40, so the $25 floor sits below the most common value. The hint should say so.

VERIFIED, NO CHANGE: CFPB report p.5 says 'Average APR for new general purpose accounts opened in 2024 was 27.5 percent'. GST is left out, and the assumption line says so.

verify.lens: safety-and-scope skeptic: advice, recommendation, product naming, promised returns, personal data, moralising, content rules, maths edge cases. Every pinned figure was re-run in node against the spec's own algorithm.
problems: P1 (maths, wrong result shown to readers, US): the 'carried' never-falls test (`carried > 0 && i >= pay`) runs in month one, when lastI = 0. So the interest-plus minimum is only 1% of the balance (or the floor), even though every later minimum adds that month's interest. Result: at the US default rule (1% + interest, $25 floor, 27.5%), every balance above $1,115.91 returns months: null with reason 'never-falls'. Re-run: $1,200 -> never-falls, but it actually clears in 96 months with $1,485.51 of interest. $10,000 -> never-falls, but it clears in 304 months with $21,032.30. $400 at 80% -> never-falls, but it clears in 46 months. The tool would tell a US reader with an ordinary card balance that the balance never falls. That is false, and it is fear framing.

P2 (wrong regulator claim, both editions): the never-falls sentence says RBI's card directions require the minimum to be set so this cannot happen. RBI MD para 9(b)(ii) only forbids negative amortisation, and its Annex says the minimum must not be less than interest plus charges. At the spec's own pin, minPercent 3.5 on 42% a year, the payment equals the interest (₹700 = ₹700) and the balance stays flat. RBI's rule permits that, so the sentence misstates RBI for that pin. The spec also gives the sentence no per-edition wording, so a US reader would be shown an Indian regulator's rule.

P3 (the tool contradicts its own always-shown fact, India): in 'statement' mode, month one charges i = b × r even when the payment covers the whole statement. With compare = ₹20,000, the full statement, the run gives 2 months and ₹724.50 of interest. With a balance of ₹150, below the ₹200 floor, it pays ₹155.25 including ₹5.25 of interest. Both contradict the fact 'paid in full by the due date … no interest', the lesson's 'Any part left unpaid is charged interest', and the edge case 'Balance at or below the floor: cleared in one payment'. RBI MD 9(b)(iii) suspends the interest-free period only when a balance from the previous bill is still outstanding.

P4 (compare check wrong, US): 'A compare amount below the first minimum' is tested only against month one. On the interest-plus rule, the minimum jumps after month one. On $10,000 it is $100 in month one and $328.15 in month two. A fixed $150 passes the check, is labelled on time, and then its own run returns never-falls. The spec has no text for a compare run that is never-falls or over 100 years, so the template '{cMonths} months' would print null.

P5 (rounding tail gives a false result): blank counts as 0 in toNumber, and the spec only rejects blank or negative values. So minFloor = 0 is allowed. A percent rule with no floor decays geometrically, and at paise level round2 makes pay equal i. Re-run India with floor 0: never-falls after 702 months at a ₹0.49 balance. Floor 0 at APR 0: never-falls after 236 months at ₹0.09. The reader would get the 'minimum does not cover the interest' or RBI sentence at 0% interest. Balance = 0 is also allowed and gives 'clears ₹0 in 0 months'. Balance has no upper cap; a 20-digit query value passes the 24-character limit and loses the 2-decimal precision round2 relies on.

P6 (undefined rounding): round2 is named but never defined. The default pins are stable across definitions, but other inputs differ by a few cents at half-cent ties, because r = apr/1200 is computed before b × r. With the P1 fix, $10,000 gives interest of 21,032.30 with Math.round(x*100)/100 and 21,032.33 with toFixed. 'Settles the one-paisa difference' is therefore not guaranteed.

P7 (content quality, sentence template): '{years} years {remMonths} months' produces '1 years 8 months' for the US default (the spec's own output line says '1 year 8 months'), '0 years 9 months' for the US compare, and '3 years 0 months'.

P8 (undisclosed simplification that understates the cost): interest is charged once a month on one balance. Real cards charge daily interest from the transaction date once the interest-free period is lost (RBI 9(b)(iii)); US cards charge on the average daily balance, with trailing interest. The assumption line leaves this out. India's GST on card interest (about 18% on top of the ₹40,332.68) is disclosed only as 'left out'. The headline interest is a floor, not an estimate, and the page does not say so.

P9 (the 'paid in full' fact is overstated): 'paid in full by the due date, the purchases on a statement usually carry no interest' is true only when nothing was carried from the previous statement (RBI 9(b)(iii); CFPB grace-period page). A reader using this tool is likely already carrying a balance.

Checked and not a problem: no buy/sell/hold, no product, card or bank named on the page (Bankrate and Khan Academy appear only in the internal modelledOn field), no promised return, no personal identifiers collected, inputs stay in the browser (the query string is written only on an explicit copy or share).
