build.title: Buffer target and the payday it is reached
build.answers: On which payday will a buffer for my must-pay costs be ready?
build.short: When will my buffer be ready?
build.intro: Answers one question: how big is a buffer for your must-pay costs, and on which payday do you have it?

inputs.label: Must-pay costs a month
inputs.hint: Rent or room share, food, getting to work or college, and your phone. Leave out what can shrink in a bad month.
inputs.source: example: the lessons' own totals, in/money-basics/one-month-buffer (₹2,500 + 1,800 + 600 + 300 + 300), eu/money-basics/three-month-buffer (€400 + 60 + 20 + 250), us/money-basics/first-cushion ($600 + 45 + 120 + 290)

inputs.label: Months to cover
inputs.hint: India's lesson starts at one month. Europe's uses three, the measure in the EU's strategy. The US lesson starts at one month, with $400 on the way.

inputs.label: Already set aside for this
inputs.hint: Only money kept apart for a bill you did not choose, not this month's spending money.

inputs.label: Moved aside each payday (the US label says 'paycheck')
inputs.hint: Moved on payday, before the first spend.
inputs.source: example: the three buffer lessons (₹2,000 a month, €185 each payday, $50 a paycheck)

inputs.label: How often you are paid (a select: weekly, every two weeks, twice a month, monthly)
inputs.hint: Turns the count of paydays into months.

outputs: Headline (Figure): the payday the target is reached, and about how many months that is. India 'Payday 3, about 3 months'; Europe 'Payday 12, about 12 months'; US 'Paycheck 22, about 10.2 months'.
Ledger: Must-pay costs, {essentials} × {months} = Buffer target (₹5,500 / €2,190 / $1,055); − Already set aside (0); double-ruled Still to set aside.
Fact: on that payday you hold ₹6,000, ₹500 past the target (Europe €2,220, €30 past; US $1,100, $45 past).
Fact, US only: $400, the Federal Reserve survey's measure of a small emergency, is reached on paycheck 8. Its source and date are shown.
Assumption line: the same amount every payday and no interest, so only the deposits do the work (at the Europe lesson's example 1%, interest adds about €10 in a year).
build.resultSentence: {months} month(s) of these costs is {target}. With {saved} already set aside and {perPayday} moved each {paydayWord}, it is reached on {paydayWord} {n}, about {approxMonths} months from now. If already covered: {saved} already covers the {target} target, with {surplus} to spare. Example (Europe): 3 months of these costs is €2,190. With €0 already set aside and €185 moved each payday, it is reached on payday 12, about 12 months from now.
build.maths: bufferPlan(essentials, months, saved, perPayday, paydaysPerYear: 52 | 26 | 24 | 12, milestone?: number): { target, toGo, paydays: number | null, approxMonths: number | null, heldAtEnd: number | null, milestonePayday: number | null }. target = round2(essentials × months). toGo = max(0, round2(target − saved)). paydays = 0 when toGo is 0; otherwise ceil(toGo / perPayday − 1e-9) when perPayday > 0, and null when it is not. approxMonths = round1(paydays × 12 / paydaysPerYear). heldAtEnd = round2(saved + paydays × perPayday). milestonePayday = ceil((milestone − saved) / perPayday − 1e-9) when milestone > saved and perPayday > 0. No interest. The US milestone (400) is a Rule in regions.ts with the Federal Reserve source. Pins: India 5,500 × 1 at 2,000 monthly gives payday 3, 3 months and ₹6,000 held. Europe 730 × 3 = 2,190 at 185 monthly gives payday 12 and €2,220. US 1,055 × 1 at 50 every two weeks gives paycheck 22, 10.2 months and $1,100, with $400 on paycheck 8, the lesson's 'the eighth'.
edgeCases: Already set aside at or above the target: 0 paydays, and the 'already covers' sentence.
0 or blank each payday: no date is shown, and the sentence asks for an amount.
Months of 0: error text ('at least 1'). Fractions such as 1.5 are allowed.
More than 600 paydays: 'more than 600 paydays at this amount' instead of a date decades away.
Negative inputs: error text under the field.
Irregular pay: How this is worked out says a smaller payday moves the date, and invites trying the smaller amount.
Interest is left out on purpose. No account type or product is named, and the deposit-guarantee facts stay in the Europe lesson.
US milestone at or below the amount saved: the milestone fact is hidden.
build.whyItHelps: All three buffer lessons work out the target and the date by hand. The Europe goal screen reads '€2,190 ÷ 12 is €182.50, rounded up … Goal reached month 12', and the US lesson says '$400 ÷ $50 is eight paychecks'. They do it by hand because the savings tool only runs forward from an amount over a number of years. 49% of EU adults aged 18–65 lack three months of savings (COM(2025) 681). 63% of US adults would cover a $400 emergency with cash or its equivalent (Federal Reserve, 13 May 2026). The India lesson opens on a loan app offering money when a ₹4,500 repair falls due.
build.modelledOn: NerdWallet's emergency fund calculator (essentials × months), crossed with Chase's time-to-goal tool (rate 0% by default) and Practical Money Skills' 'already enough' state. What is different: months is the reader's input, set by default to the lesson's. There is no 'should', no 'are you able to save this?' branch and no rate field, and the $400 comes from a dated federal survey.
risks: A prescriptive target: months is an input, the sentence says 'is', never 'should', and $400 is labelled as the survey's measure, not a rule.
Moralising about wants: the hint says wants can shrink, not that they are wrong.
Product drift: nothing is said about where to keep the money.
Same amount every payday: the assumption is stated under the result.
The judges agreed on this tool; there was nothing to settle.
build.effort: small: src/lib/finance.ts (bufferPlan) + tests; src/islands/BufferTarget.tsx (about 90 lines, about 2–3 KB gz); tool-kit SelectField (shared with take-home-pay); src/lib/regions.ts (buffer per edition, the US milestone Rule, paydayWord); src/lib/tools.ts; [tool].astro; e2e; frontmatter of the three buffer lessons.

verify.lens: Safety and scope: advice, recommendation, named product, promised return, personal data, moralising, content-rule failures, and maths edge cases (zero, negative, huge, non-integer, rate 0, months 0), checked against the repo on branch complete-and-redesign
problems: Switching the lessons' frontmatter breaks two of them. The spec changes the `tool:` of all three buffer lessons, but `tool` is one optional string (src/content/schema.ts:233). LessonLayout.astro:330 passes `d.tool` to GrowthExplorer. In in/money-basics/one-month-buffer and eu/money-basics/three-month-buffer the explorable is `kind: growth`, and its button (GrowthExplorer.tsx:83) reads 'Open the savings calculator with these numbers' with ?start&monthly&rate&years. After the switch that button opens buffer-target, which ignores those keys, under a label that names a different calculator. India's objectives 2 and 3 (compound growth, interest on debt) would also lose their tool link.

The US $400 milestone is tied to dollars, but the currency can be changed. The calculators share CurrencyField (tool-kit.tsx:91) and remember lp:locale, so a US reader who picks INR or EUR, or has one saved, would see '₹400 / €400, the Federal Reserve survey's measure … paycheck 8'. That is false, and it attaches a named regulator's survey to the wrong figure.

The Europe assumption line hard-codes 'at the Europe lesson's example 1%, interest adds about €10 in a year'. The €10 is right only for €185 a month over 12 months (checked: 185 × 12.0552 − 2,220 ≈ €10.2). Once the reader changes an input or the currency, the line shows a stale or wrong figure next to their own result, and it adds a rate claim to a tool that has no rate field.

The spec does not handle essentials of 0 or blank. toNumber('') is 0, so target = 0, toGo = 0 and paydays = 0, and the page says '₹0 already covers the ₹0 target, with ₹0 to spare'. The edge cases cover months 0 and negatives but not essentials ≤ 0.

The payday frequency comes from an unvalidated select. useFields/readQuery (tool-kit.tsx:26-35) accept any query value up to 24 characters. `?paidEvery=fortnightly` gives paydaysPerYear undefined, so approxMonths is NaN ('about NaN months') and the select shows no matching option. The option values in the spec ('every two weeks') also contain spaces.
The spec gives no headline for the 'already covered' state. The Figure is defined as 'the payday the target is reached', so with paydays = 0 it would print 'Payday 0, about 0 months'.

The milestone is hidden only when it is at or below the amount saved. If a US reader's target is under $400 (essentials 300 × 1), the page reports the target on paycheck 6 and '$400 … on paycheck 8' afterwards, a milestone beyond the goal. The spec also says nothing about the milestone when perPayday is 0 (null) or when it passes the 600-payday cap.

The essentials hint contradicts itself: it lists food, then says 'Leave out what can shrink in a bad month'. The Europe lesson's own document says food 'Can shrink a little in a hard month, never to nothing. An essential.' A reader who follows the hint drops food and understates the target.

The months hint is one string for every edition. On the India page it cites 'Europe's uses three, the measure in the EU's strategy' and 'the US lesson … $400', and the EUR-Lex URL is its source in every edition. Europe's line also sits next to the default of 3, where it reads like an official recommendation. The Commission uses three months as a survey measure.

The 600-payday cap is counted in paydays, so it means different spans by pay frequency: 600 weekly paydays is about 11.5 years, 600 monthly paydays is 50 years. A monthly earner is shown dates up to 50 years away, which the spec itself calls 'decades away'.

No field has a maximum. A 20-digit entry gives a figure too wide for the 360px ledger (WCAG 1.4.10 reflow); an extreme entry gives Infinity, which Intl formats as '₹∞'. Months has no upper bound. Months below 1 is ambiguous: the spec says 'Months of 0: error (at least 1)' and 'fractions such as 1.5 are allowed', and says nothing of 0.5.

Precedence between errors and results is not specified. A negative perPayday with saved ≥ target gives an error under the field and the 'already covers' sentence at the same time, because paydays = 0 is decided before perPayday is checked.

Parts of the build do not exist in the repo. regions.ts has no 'Rule' type (only Stat and Source). tool-kit.tsx has no SelectField, and 'take-home-pay', which it is said to share with, does not exist. [tool].astro keeps a per-slug `scenario` record, and without a buffer-target entry the 'It opens on an example' line is missing, which breaks the 'opens on a per-edition example' rule.

The copy has faults. The sentence prints 'month(s)' and 'about 1 months'. 'with {surplus} to spare' reads as permission to spend the surplus. 'about N months from now' assumes the next payday is a full pay period away, and the assumption line does not say so. The milestone Fact calls $400 'a small emergency'; the Fed's release says '$400 emergency expense', and the lesson calls it 'not a rule'.

The `modelledOn` field names NerdWallet, Chase and Practical Money Skills. If any of that reaches the page, the tool names real financial firms, and content rules forbid naming or referencing a real bank or app.
fixes: Leave `tool: savings` on in/money-basics/one-month-buffer and eu/money-basics/three-month-buffer, and switch only us/money-basics/first-cushion to `tool: buffer-target` (its explorable is a deduction and takes no toolHref). Better: add an optional `alsoTool: z.string().optional()` to the schema, set `alsoTool: buffer-target` on the India and Europe lessons, render it as a second plain 'Work out your own buffer date' link after the Try-it block, and include lessons where `l.data.tool === slug || l.data.alsoTool === slug` in `related` in [tool].astro. In either case, set the GrowthExplorer href in LessonLayout.astro to `${prefix}/tools/savings`, since only that tool runs the growth calculation.

Store the milestone as `milestone: { amount: 400, currency: 'USD', label: 'the emergency expense the Federal Reserve survey asks about, not a rule', source: { title: 'Economic Well-Being of U.S. Households in 2025 (13 May 2026)', url: 'https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/pressreleases/other20260513a.htm' } }`. Render the Fact only when `locale.currency === milestone.currency`.

Remove the €10 clause. The assumption line becomes: 'The same amount every payday, and no interest counted, so the date comes from your transfers alone. To see what interest adds, use the savings calculator' (a link to /<edition>/tools/savings). Do not show a rate or an interest figure in this tool.

Add a rule for essentials: must be > 0. When it is 0 or blank, show the error 'Enter your must-pay costs for one month' under the field, show no Figure or ledger, and add a unit test: bufferPlan(0, 1, 0, 100, 12) returns target 0, and the island shows the error, not 'already covers'.

Use short slug values for the select: `weekly` → 52, `biweekly` → 26, `semimonthly` → 24, `monthly` → 12, with a fixed map `PAYDAYS_PER_YEAR`. Any other value, from a query, the DOM or a default, falls back to the edition default before it reaches bufferPlan. Add an e2e test: `us/tools/buffer-target?paidEvery=fortnightly` shows 'Paycheck 22'. Build SelectField in tool-kit.tsx now (label, hint, options, aria-describedby), matching NumberField.

In the covered state the Figure reads 'Covered now' with the label 'Already set aside is at or above the target'. The ledger closes on 'Still to set aside: ₹0', and the sentence is '{saved} already covers the {target} target, {surplus} above it.' The payday count and months line are hidden.

Show the milestone Fact only when all four hold: saved < milestone.amount < target, perPayday > 0, milestonePayday ≤ the cap, and the currency matches. Add unit tests: target 300 (hidden), saved 400 (hidden), perPayday 0 (null).
New essentials hint: 'Rent or room share, food, getting to work or college, and your phone: what still has to be paid in a month with no pay. Leave out spending that would stop.'

Make the months hint per edition, in regions.ts. India: 'The lesson starts at one month of costs.' Europe: 'The lesson uses three months, the measure the European Commission's 2025 strategy reports on, not a rule.' US: 'The lesson starts at one month; $400 is shown on the way.' Only the Europe hint cites the EUR-Lex source.

Cap on time, not on payday count: if approxMonths > 120, show 'more than 10 years at {perPayday} each {paydayWord}; a larger amount brings the date closer' and hide the payday number. Unit-test the cap at weekly and at monthly pay.

Set limits and error text. Essentials, saved and perPayday: 0 ≤ x ≤ 1e9 ('This works with amounts up to 1,000,000,000'). Months: 1 ≤ x ≤ 24, fractions allowed ('Enter between 1 and 24 months'), so 0.5 is an error. Pass max= to NumberField. Guard `Number.isFinite` in bufferPlan and return nulls when the input is not finite. For the payday count, prefer integer cents (`Math.ceil(Math.round(toGo*100) / Math.round(perPayday*100))`) to the 1e-9 epsilon.

If any field has an error, render only the error texts and a line 'Fix the field marked above to see the date'; show no Figure, ledger or sentence. Unit-test and e2e-test with saved ≥ target and perPayday = −5.

In regions.ts, add `buffer: { essentials, months, saved, perPayday, paidEvery, paydayWord: 'payday' | 'paycheck', monthsHint, scenario, milestone? }` to ToolDefaults. Add `'buffer-target': t.buffer.scenario` to the scenario record in [tool].astro, one per edition. For example, India: 'Five costs from a month of part-time pay, ₹5,500, with ₹2,000 moved aside each payday.' Drop the 'shared with take-home-pay' dependency from the effort estimate.

Plural rules: '1 month', '1.5 months', 'about 1 month'. Replace 'to spare' with 'above it'. Headline label: 'about N months of paydays, counting from your next one'. The assumption line adds: 'Counted from your next payday.' Milestone wording: '$400, the emergency expense the Federal Reserve's survey asks about (not a rule), is passed on paycheck 8, about 3.7 months.'

Treat `modelledOn` and `whyItHelps` as internal notes. No text naming NerdWallet, Chase, Practical Money Skills or any other firm goes into tools.ts, regions.ts, the island or 'How this is worked out'.

verify.lens: Skeptic: I checked the sources, the rules, the maths pins and how the spec fits the existing code. What held up: the Fed's household survey (SHED) says 63% would cover a $400 emergency expense with cash or its equivalent, unchanged from 2024; it was fielded in October 2025 and published 13 May 2026, and it calls these "relatively small, unexpected expenses". The EU figure of 49% of adults aged 18 to 65 without enough emergency savings for at least three months without borrowing comes from the 2023 Eurobarometer and is cited in COM(2025) 681; the EUR-Lex HTML and PDF came back empty to the fetcher, so I confirmed it through the PDF's search snippet and ABBL. Every pin recomputes: India payday 3 with ₹6,000 held, Europe payday 12 with €2,220, US paycheck 22 with $1,100, $400 on paycheck 8, and €10.20 of interest at 1%. The savings tool really has no goal mode. The problems below are in the display, the wording and the code wiring, not in the core maths.
problems: The $400 milestone can print in the wrong currency. The currency choice is saved in lp:locale for every edition (useLocale in src/islands/tool-kit.tsx), and switching edition never resets it. A reader who once picked India (₹) or Europe (€) sees the US page formatted in that currency, so the Fact would read '₹400, the Federal Reserve survey's measure'. That is a false statement a real reader can reach.

The months hint misstates the EU source. 'Europe's uses three, the measure in the EU's strategy' reads as if the EU recommends three months. COM(2025) 681 only reports a 2023 Eurobarometer result: 49% of those aged 18 to 65 lack emergency savings to cover living expenses for 'at least three months, without borrowing'. It sets no target. whyItHelps also drops 'without borrowing'.

The US hint gets the lesson's order backwards. It says the US lesson 'starts at one month, with $400 on the way'. first-cushion.mdx says the opposite: 'Start with $400', and a month of must-pay costs ($1,055) is 'the second target'.

approxMonths claims more precision than it has, and 'from now' can be off by up to one pay period. round1(paydays × 12 / paydaysPerYear) assumes payday 1 is a full period away. If you are paid today (the US lesson opens 'Today your $640 paycheck landed'), paycheck 22 is 21 × 14 = 294 days away, about 9.7 months, not '10.2 months from now'. Short cases also read badly: 1 twice-a-month payday gives 'about 0.5 months'. Singular cases print 'about 1 months' and '1 month(s)'.

Changing the lessons' frontmatter breaks their explorables. A lesson has one `tool` (schema: z.string().optional()), and LessonLayout.astro also uses it as the explorable's toolHref. India's and Europe's buffer lessons use GrowthExplorer, which is compound growth at a rate. Setting tool: buffer-target would send that growth explorer's calculator link to a tool with no rate field. Keeping tool: savings leaves the new tool with no 'Lessons that use this', because [tool].astro filters on l.data.tool === tool.slug.

The spec relies on code that does not exist. regions.ts has no `Rule` type (only Source and Stat), and ToolDefaults has no buffer entry or paydayWord. There is no SelectField in tool-kit.tsx, and the take-home-pay tool it would be 'shared with' is not built. The effort estimate leaves these out.

The paidEvery select takes unchecked input from a shared link. readQuery in tool-kit accepts any string of 24 characters or fewer for every key, and the spec uses labels ('every two weeks') as values. A crafted link could set an unknown frequency, so paydaysPerYear would be undefined and the result NaN. SECURITY.md row 11 requires values from a link to be checked by shape.

The $400 Fact risks overstating what the survey measured. The Fed's 'cash or its equivalent' includes 'a credit card paid off at the next statement', so the 63% are not people with $400 saved. The spec's 'measure of a small emergency' also needs the survey's own words ('a hypothetical expense of $400') and the October 2025 fieldwork date.

The milestone shows even when it is above the target. If the target is under $400 (say essentials of $300 × 1), the target is reached on paycheck 6 and the Fact then says $400 arrives on paycheck 8. The two lines contradict each other. The spec hides the milestone only when it is at or below the amount saved.
The 600-payday cap means different spans at different pay frequencies: 11.5 years for weekly pay, 50 years for monthly.

The months limits contradict each other. The error text says 'at least 1', but 'fractions such as 1.5 are allowed', so 0.5 is undefined. There is no upper cap, while the savings tool has MAX_YEARS = 50.
The assumption line hard-codes '(at the Europe lesson's example 1%, interest adds about €10 in a year)'. It goes wrong as soon as the inputs change, and it means nothing in the India or US edition.

The ledger stops at 'Still to set aside', so it never reaches the headline answer (the payday count). The division and round-up (€2,190 ÷ €185 = 11.84, rounded up to 12) and the amount held on that payday are not in the ledger.
India's essentials hint lists rent, food, travel and phone, but the ₹5,500 default also includes 'Course materials ₹300' from one-month-buffer.mdx. The default does not match its own hint.

modelledOn cannot be verified. I found no Chase 'time-to-goal tool (rate 0% by default)': the chase.com short-term goals page only has a worked example, and the savings calculator at tools.chase.com could not be confirmed. Practical Money Skills' 'already enough' state was not checked. None of this is shown to readers, but it is an unsourced claim in the spec.
fixes: Put the milestone data on the US edition as `milestone: { amount: 400, currency: 'USD', ... }`. Render the Fact only when region.code === 'us' AND locale.currency === 'USD'. Otherwise hide it and show nothing in its place. Print the amount from the rule as the literal '$400', never through money() in the current locale.

Change the hint to: 'Europe's lesson uses three: the length the EU's 2023 survey asked about, reported in its 2025 strategy.' List Flash Eurobarometer 525 (https://europa.eu/eurobarometer/surveys/detail/2953) as a source next to COM(2025) 681. build.title: Pay-later plans against one payday
build.answers: What is left of this payday once my pay-later plans take their share?
build.short: What do my pay-later plans leave?
build.intro: Answers one question: after living costs and every pay-later payment due today, what is left of this pay?

inputs.label: Pay arriving this payday
inputs.hint: What reaches your account: net pay, or take-home on the paycheck.

inputs.label: Living costs from this pay
inputs.hint: Rent, bills, food, transport and phone.

inputs.label: Moved to savings on payday
inputs.hint: Leave at 0 if nothing moves.

inputs.label: Payments due this payday, one row per plan (up to four), each with the number of payments left after this one
inputs.hint: Only payments that leave on this payday. Rows are named Plan 1 to Plan 4: no shop or lender names.
inputs.source: example: the lessons' plans (trainers, coat, books; headphones, jacket, shoes), each on 'payment 2 of 4'

outputs: Headline (Figure): left for the month (€306) or left for the next two weeks ($323).
Ledger, Europe: Pay €1,200; − Living costs €804; = Left after living costs €396; − Plan 1 €30; − Plan 2 €36; − Plan 3 €24; double-ruled Left for the month €306.
Ledger, US: Pay $1,317; − Living costs $817; − Moved to savings $132; = Left after living costs $368; − Plan 1 $15; − Plan 2 $15; − Plan 3 $15; double-ruled Left for the next two weeks $323.
Fact: the plans take €90, 7.5% of this pay ($45, 3.4%).
Fact: owed on these plans with today's payments counted, €270 ($135), the lessons' 'still owed' line; after today, €180 ($90).
Fact: fee if a payment fails. €15 is the example on the Europe lesson's screen; US fees were often around $7 (CFPB, 2022). Each plan's terms set the real fee.
build.resultSentence: After living costs and {count} {instalmentWord}s, {left} is left of {pay}. The plans take {plansTotal}, {share}% of this pay, and {owedAfter} is still due on them after today. If short: This pay is {shortfall} short once the {instalmentWord}s come out. Example (Europe): After living costs and 3 instalments, €306 is left of €1,200. The plans take €90, 7.5% of this pay, and €180 is still due on them after today.
build.maths: paydayAfterPlans(pay, living, savings, plans: { amount: number; left: number }[]): DeductionResult & { plansTotal; share: number | null; owedIncludingToday; owedAfter }. It runs deductions(pay, lines). lines = [{ label: 'Living costs', amount: living }, then { label: 'Moved to savings', amount: savings } only when savings > 0, then ...plans.map((p, i) => ({ label: `Plan ${i + 1}`, amount: p.amount }))]; the line before Plan 1 carries subtotalLabel 'Left after living costs'. plansTotal = round2(Σ amount). share = round1(plansTotal / pay × 100) when pay > 0, otherwise null. owedAfter = round2(Σ amount × left). owedIncludingToday = round2(Σ amount × (left + 1)). Both assume each remaining payment equals this one, as in pay-in-four. In a copied link, rows go after the # as plans=30~2|36~2|24~2: at most 4 rows, each part numeric and 12 characters or fewer, validated in a small codec beside budget-link.ts. Pins: Europe 1,200 − 804 − 30 − 36 − 24 = 306, share 7.5, owed 270 and 180. US 1,317 − 817 − 132 − 15 − 15 − 15 = 323, share 3.4, owed 135 and 90.
edgeCases: Left below zero: shown in the loss style, with the 'short' sentence and no 'you overspent'.
No plans: the figure is pay minus living costs, and the sentence says no payments are due.
A fifth plan: rows are capped at four, with a note to add the rest to living costs.
0 left on every plan: the sentence says these are the last payments.
Pay of 0 or blank: the share is hidden, and a prompt asks for the pay.
Plans that charge interest or were extended are not modelled; a link points to the loan tool.
Plans on a different schedule from pay: How this is worked out says 'after today' counts the payments still to come, not their dates.
EU late-fee caps are national (the revised Consumer Credit Directive applies from 20 Nov 2026); that line goes in How this is worked out.
build.whyItHelps: The CFPB (Jan 2025) found most pay-in-four borrowers at six lenders had more than one loan at once, and 37% of 18–24-year-olds had used one. The AFM counted about 53 million Dutch pay-later transactions in 2024. REGIONAL_TEACHING lists 'BNPL is a loan' for Europe and a BNPL basket for the US. The research sweep found no pay-later calculator at Chase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo, Capital One, NerdWallet, Bankrate or Citi. Both lessons already run this exact deduction, but only on three fixed pay figures and the lesson's own plans, and their deduction explorable links to no tool, so a reader cannot type in their own plans.
build.modelledOn: The two lessons' deduction explorers and BudgetPlanner's add and remove rows; NerdWallet's small capped 'add another' rows. What is different: no provider names and no mascot, and 0% is stated as 0% without calling it free or costly. It shows one payday, not a scripted run of paydays.
risks: Anti-BNPL moralising: amounts and shares only, never 'avoid'. Chosen over proposal 1's multi-payday simulation, whose scripted 'add one more purchase' step both judges rejected.
Late fees vary: the fee is an example with its source, and the plan's terms set the real fee.
Named shops or lenders: rows are Plan 1 to 4, and no free text is stored or put in a link.
Privacy: pay and plans in a copied link go after the #.
build.effort: medium: src/lib/finance.ts (paydayAfterPlans) + tests; src/islands/PayLaterPayday.tsx (about 130 lines with rows, about 3–4 KB gz); a plans codec (src/lib/plans-link.ts, beside budget-link.ts) + tests; src/lib/regions.ts (eu and us payLater, including instalmentWord 'instalment'/'installment', period wording and failFee with its source); src/lib/tools.ts (regions ['eu','us']); [tool].astro; e2e (add and remove a row by keyboard at 360px); frontmatter of both BNPL lessons.

verify.lens: safety-and-scope skeptic: advice, recommendation, named products, promised returns, personal data, moralising, content rules, and maths edge cases, checked against src/lib/finance.ts, src/islands/tool-kit.tsx, src/lib/tools.ts, src/pages/[region]/tools/[tool].astro, src/layouts/LessonLayout.astro and both BNPL lessons
problems: The result sentence is wrong on the tool's own US default. The template 'After living costs and {count} {instalmentWord}s, {left} is left of {pay}' leaves out savings, so it reads 'After living costs and 3 installments, $323 is left of $1,317'. But $1,317 − $817 − $45 = $455; the missing $132 is the savings line.

The US ledger mislabels its subtotal. The spec puts subtotalLabel 'Left after living costs' on the line before Plan 1, which is the savings line when savings > 0. So the $368 is labelled as if savings had not come out. The US lesson labels these 'After living costs' ($500) and 'After savings' ($368).

The privacy claim does not match the shared kit. ToolActions in src/islands/tool-kit.tsx writes every input to url.search, and useFields reads only the query string. As specified, pay, living costs and savings would travel in the query string and only the plans would go after the #. The risk line 'pay and plans in a copied link go after the #' is untrue unless the kit changes, and tool-kit.tsx is not in the effort list.

It undercounts when plans and pay run on different schedules. The row counts only 'payments that leave on this payday'. A reader paid monthly with two-weekly pay-in-four plans has a second instalment from each plan before the next pay, and the tool leaves it out. The headline 'Left for the month' then overstates what is left, which is the one thing the tool exists to answer. The edge-case note only fixes the wording of the owed figure, not the headline.

The headline period wording is fixed per edition. 'Left for the next two weeks' (US) and 'Left for the month' (EU) assume a pay frequency. US readers paid weekly, twice a month or monthly get a wrong label.

The 'payments left after this one' input is error-prone and not validated. The plan screens in both lessons show 'Payment 2 of 4', so readers will type 2 or 4 instead of working out 4 − 2. The spec also does not require a whole number or a floor of 0: 'left' = 2.5 or −1 gives nonsense owed figures, and 999999999999 (12 characters) passes the codec. toNumber() keeps a '-' sign, so negative instalments, pay, living costs or savings would be added to what is left instead of taken off. NumberField's min='0' is not enforced as the reader types.

The codec rule 'each part numeric and 12 characters or fewer' is loose. Number() accepts '0x1F', '1e9', 'Infinity', '-5' and '' (as 0). The existing budget-link.ts decode keeps '-', so it is the wrong model to copy.
Pluralisation breaks: '{count} {instalmentWord}s' gives '1 instalments'. Count is also undefined for a row left at 0 or blank, so an empty added row would be counted as an instalment.

The shortfall sentence can blame the plans for a gap they did not cause. 'This pay is {shortfall} short once the instalments come out' also fires when living costs plus savings already exceed pay before any plan, and when there are no plans at all.
The owed wording 'still due on them after today' assumes the reader uses the tool on payday. Both lessons set the scene before payday ('before 1 October', 'before Friday').

The share is written as '{share}%' with a hard-coded symbol and a round1 value. It ignores the kit's locale-aware percent() formatter, so a reader who picks pt-BR sees '7.5%' instead of '7,5%'. finance.ts exports no round1 or round2; round2 is private to lesson-math.ts.

The €15 fee sits under a 'Fact:' label but is a made-up example from a made-up screen, and its 'source' is that same lesson screen, which is circular. The US line 'often around $7 (CFPB, 2022)' misquotes the source the lesson cites: in 2021 the three large lenders that charged late fees set them at $7 or $8, per the September 2022 report. It also drops the bank's overdraft or NSF fee that the US lesson names, and 'CFPB' reaches the reader as an unexplained acronym.

Capping rows at four and telling the reader to 'add the rest to living costs' makes the plans' share and both owed figures understate the debt for exactly the readers with the most plans. The CFPB found that about 63% of borrowers at six firms had more than one loan at once.

The page template treats any tool with a regions list as a drill. [tool].astro sets kind={tool.regions ? 'Practice' : 'Calculator'}, which feeds the Pagefind 'kind' filter, so this calculator would be indexed as 'Practice'. It also sets regionSub to 'tools', so the edition menu on /eu/tools/pay-later-payday sends the reader to /us/tools instead of /us/tools/pay-later-payday.
The spec requires the tool to 'open on a per-edition example', but [tool].astro's scenario map has no entry for this slug. The 'It opens on an example' line would not render.

The lesson link the spec cites as the reason for building this ('their deduction explorable links to no tool') is not fixed by the effort list. DeductionExplorer.tsx has no toolHref prop, and LessonLayout.astro passes none for kind 'deduction'. Changing the frontmatter from tool: budget only moves the two lessons from the budget page's list to this page's list. Also, both lessons already link to the budget planner, where a reader can type in their own plans as rows. The spec never says what this tool does that the budget planner does not.

whyItHelps overstates two claims. The 37% is 18–24-year-olds in the CFPB's credit-record sample who financed at least one purchase with BNPL in 2022 (report of January 2025), not a general 'had used one'. NerdWallet does publish an installment-loan calculator pitched at BNPL. The accurate claim is that no calculator adds several plans against one payday.
Keyboard behaviour for adding and removing rows is not specified: where focus goes and what is announced. Only an e2e test is named.
fixes: Make the sentence name every line that came off: 'After living costs{savings > 0 ? ", savings" : ""} and {count} {instalment|instalments}, {left} is left of {pay}.' Pin the test: US gives 'After living costs, savings and 3 installments, $323 is left of $1,317.'

Label the subtotals as the US lesson does: 'Left after living costs' on the living-costs line, then 'Left after savings' on the savings line when savings > 0. The line before Plan 1 always carries whichever of the two it is. Pin both editions' ledgers in finance.test.ts.

Add tool-kit.tsx to the effort list. Give ToolActions and useFields an opt-in 'hash' mode: write every input (pay, living, savings, plans, currency) to url.hash, set url.search to '', and read from location.hash on mount, ignoring any hash the codec rejects, such as '#main'. Add an e2e test that the copied link has no '?' and that the page restores from the hash. If the kit does not change, delete the privacy claim.

Give each row three whole-number fields: the instalment amount a; 'Payment __ of __' (k of n), exactly as the plan's screen shows it; and 'Payments due before your next pay' d (select 1, 2 or 3, default 1). Taken from this pay = a × d. Left after those = n − k − d + 1, which must be ≥ 0, validated as k ≥ 1, n ≥ k, k + d − 1 ≤ n. Owed including this pay = a × (n − k + 1). Owed after = a × (n − k − d + 1). Defaults are k = 2, n = 4, d = 1, so the pins stay: €306, 7.5%, owed €270 and €180; $323, 3.4%, owed $135 and $90. Codec row: 'a~k~n~d'.
Use one headline label in both editions, 'Left until your next pay', and remove the per-edition period wording from regions.ts.

Validate every input in finance.ts and the island. Pay, living, savings and instalment amounts are finite, ≥ 0 and ≤ 10,000,000. k, n and d are integers, 1 ≤ k ≤ n ≤ 48, d between 1 and 3. Anything outside shows an inline error tied with aria-describedby ('An instalment cannot be below 0', 'Payment number must be a whole number no higher than the total') and is treated as 0 or excluded. Unit-test −30, 2.5, 0, blank and 1e12.

Write the codec with strict regexes, not Number(): amount /^\d{1,8}(\.\d{1,2})?$/, k and n /^\d{1,2}$/, d /^[1-3]$/. Drop any row that fails, cap the number of rows, and drop the whole hash value if nothing survives. Unit-test '0x1F', '1e9', 'Infinity', '-5', '' and a 5 KB string.

Take the word from regions.ts as a pair, instalment/instalments (EU) and installment/installments (US), and choose by count (or use Intl.PluralRules). Count only rows with an amount > 0. Blank or 0 rows still show in the ledger, numbered in order, and are not counted.

Use three branches for the short case. If what is left after living costs and savings is below 0: '{living + savings} is more than this pay of {pay}, before any plan, by {gap}.' If it goes below 0 only once plans are taken off: 'This pay is {shortfall} short once the {instalments} come out.' If pay is 0 or blank: show only the prompt for the pay. None of these says 'overspent', 'avoid' or 'cut'.
Replace 'after today' with 'after this pay's {instalments}' in the sentence, the Fact label and How this is worked out.

Format the share with percent(plansTotal / pay, locale, 1) and hide it when pay ≤ 0. Add exported round1 and round2 helpers to finance.ts, or reuse the rounding that deductions() already does, and test them.

Relabel the fee line 'Example fee if a payment fails' and word it per edition. EU: '€15 in this example; each plan's terms set the real amount, and limits on late fees differ by EU country.' US: 'In 2021 the three large lenders that charged late fees set them at $7 or $8 a missed payment (Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, September 2022); your bank can add an overdraft or non-sufficient-funds fee.' Link the CFPB report the US lesson already cites. Never put a made-up figure under 'Fact'.

Raise the cap to 8 rows, in MAX_PLAN_ROWS shared by the island and the codec, and drop the 'add the rest to living costs' advice. At the cap, disable 'Add a plan' with visible text: 'Eight plans is the most this tool holds; the share and owed figures cover these eight only.'

Add kind: 'calculator' | 'practice' to ToolMeta and set it on every entry. In [tool].astro set kind={tool.kind === 'practice' ? 'Practice' : 'Calculator'}, and base regionSub on kind, not on regions. For a calculator missing from some editions, have RegionTabs fall back to 'tools' only for the editions that lack it: pass a list of available editions, or compute the tail per edition. Add an e2e test that the edition menu on /eu/tools/pay-later-payday leads to /us/tools/pay-later-payday and to /in/tools.

Add a per-edition scenario in regions.ts, used by [tool].astro's scenario map. EU: 'Three pay-later plans, each on payment 2 of 4, due on a €1,200 payday.' US: 'Three pay-in-four plans of $15, each on payment 2 of 4, due on a $1,317 payday.' No shop or lender names.

Add DeductionExplorer.tsx and LessonLayout.astro to the effort list. Give DeductionExplorer an optional toolHref, passed only when d.tool is set, so payslip lessons with no tool get no link. Set tool: pay-later-payday in both BNPL lessons. Add one line to How this is worked out saying what this tool adds over the budget planner: the payments counted per plan before the next pay, and what is still owed after them. Add a link from the budget planner to it.

Reword whyItHelps: '37% of 18–24-year-olds in the CFPB's credit-record sample financed at least one purchase with buy now, pay later in 2022 (report of 13 January 2025)' and 'no calculator found that adds several plans against one payday'.

Specify keyboard behaviour. After 'Add a plan', focus the new row's amount. After 'Remove Plan n', focus the next row's amount, or 'Add a plan' if none is left, and announce 'Plan n removed' in the role='status' line. Each remove button's accessible name includes its plan number. Test both at 360px with the keyboard only.

verify.lens: skeptic: facts, sources, per-state and per-country variation, maths, and fit with the codebase (src/lib/finance.ts, src/islands/tool-kit.tsx, src/lib/budget-link.ts, the two BNPL lessons)
problems: P1 (maths, wrong output): the resultSentence leaves out savings. With the US defaults it reads 'After living costs and 3 installments, $323 is left of $1,317'. But 1,317 - 817 - 45 = 455. The missing $132 moved to savings is what gets you to 323, so the one plain-language sentence does not add up for the US edition's own opening example.

P2 (maths/label): in the US ledger, the subtotal after '- Moved to savings $132' is labelled 'Left after living costs $368'. That figure is after living costs AND savings. The US lesson labels the same point 'After savings'.

P3 (the model is wrong for most readers): 'Only payments that leave on this payday' plus a fixed period per edition ('left for the next two weeks' for the US) assumes pay-in-four dates fall on payday. BLS CES (February 2023) puts US private establishments at 43.0% biweekly, 27.0% weekly, 19.8% semimonthly and 10.3% monthly. Pay-in-four is due every two weeks (CFPB 2022). A semimonthly or monthly payer can have two instalments per plan before the next pay, and those instalments fall between paydays. For a weekly payer, 'next two weeks' is the wrong period. The tool then overstates what is left. Most EU pay is monthly, but plan schedules vary (30-day, monthly and fortnightly), so the same undercount applies there.

P4 (stale US figure): 'US fees were often around $7 (CFPB, 2022)' describes 2021 data. The report's Table 3 gives $8 (capped), $7 (capped) and $7 per missed payment in 2021. The CFPB's newer report, 'The Buy Now, Pay Later Market' (10 December 2025, data to 2023, four lenders), gives an average late fee assessed of $9.70 nominal in 2023 ($9.99 inflation-adjusted) and an average collected of $5.70. Late fees were assessed on 4.1% of loans. The $7 figure is superseded.

P5 (US varies by state, and the spec is silent on it): the CFPB 2022 report says late fees 'may vary' by the borrower's state of residence. One lender limited them only in two states where the law requires a limit. New York's BNPL Act (May 2025) has DFS rules proposed on 15 July 2026, including an $8 late-fee cap. The comment period closed on 14 September 2026, and the rules take effect 180 days after adoption, so they are not yet in force. The spec flags national variation for the EU only.

P6 (label mismatch): the row is called 'Fee if a payment fails', but the cited US figure is a late fee. In the CFPB's 2022 report, two of three lenders charged it at 10 days past due. A failed autopay attempt can instead bring a bank overdraft or NSF fee. The US lesson screen says 'Late fee, if one is missed'. The EU €15 is an example the lesson made up, with no source.

P7 (source wording, whyItHelps): the Jan 2025 CFPB report describes 2022 data. The '37% of 18-24-year-olds' figure is about 37% of consumers aged 18-24 with a credit record who financed at least one purchase with one of six large lenders in 2022, not all 18-24-year-olds. 'Most ... had more than one loan at once' is 'about 63% originated multiple simultaneous loans at some point during 2022'. The data year and the population are missing.

P8 (source claim partly wrong): 'no pay-later calculator at ... NerdWallet'. NerdWallet's Installment Loan Calculator (nerdwallet.com/personal-loans/calculators/installment-loan) has a 'Buy now, pay later loans' section. It handles one loan in years and has no add-another rows, so 'modelledOn: NerdWallet's small capped add another rows' does not match that page and has no named source.

P9 (edge case corrupts the headline facts): the 'fifth plan: add the rest to living costs' workaround takes those plans out of plansTotal, share, owedIncludingToday and owedAfter, which are the figures this tool exists to show. The cap of four is also low: the CFPB (Jan 2025) found about 20% of borrowers financed more than one purchase a month.

P10 (clashes with the existing kit, effort underestimated): the spec puts pay and plans after the '#'. But src/islands/tool-kit.tsx ToolActions builds links with url.search, and useFields/readQuery reads window.location.search. BudgetPlanner reads ?rows= the same way. As specified, either the share link ignores the hash or the kit must change, and tool-kit.tsx is not in the effort list. PROJECT_BRIEF §6 also says the query string.

P11 (type mismatch): the maths gives the line before Plan 1 a subtotalLabel, but finance.ts DeductionLine is { label; amount } only. subtotalLabel exists in lesson-math.ts DeductionNumbers, not in finance.ts, so the spec's lines array does not match the deductions() signature.

P12 (codec gap): 'each part numeric and 12 characters or fewer' still admits negative, fractional, huge or NaN-ish 'left' counts, for example 30~-2 or 30~1e9. The owed figures then come out negative or absurd.

P13 (inaccurate premise): 'their deduction explorable links to no tool'. Both lessons set tool: budget in frontmatter, so they already link to the budget planner. The change is a swap, not an addition, and the budget planner loses those two lesson links.

P14 (EU wording is imprecise; EUR-Lex text not retrievable here, so this rests on a search snippet of Article 35): the revised CCD does not make late-fee caps national as such. Article 35 lets member states require that default charges be no greater than the lender's costs. Article 31 requires caps on interest, APR or total cost of credit, or equivalent measures. The 20 November 2026 application date is confirmed by the Commission page. The 53 million, €5.1bn and 1.8 million AFM figures are confirmed (July 2025).
fixes: F1: resultSentence becomes 'After living costs{savings > 0 ? `, ${savingsAmount} to savings` : ''} and {count} {instalmentWord}s, {left} is left of {pay}.' Add a unit test pinning the US default string: 'After living costs, $132 to savings and 3 installments, $323 is left of $1,317.'
F2: subtotal label is 'Left after living costs' when savings = 0 and 'Left after living costs and savings' when savings > 0. The pinned US ledger reads '= Left after living costs and savings $368'.

F3: change the question to 'What is left of this pay once my pay-later plans take their share before the next payday?' Plans input hint: 'Every payment that leaves before your next pay arrives, not just today's.' Each row becomes { amount per payment, dueBeforeNextPay: whole number 1-4 (default 1), leftAfter: whole number 0-12 }. The ledger line for a row is amount x dueBeforeNextPay, labelled 'Plan n (2 payments)' when more than 1. build.answers: Would I catch a payment scam before I tapped?
build.short: Would I catch a payment scam?
build.intro: Made-up screens, real patterns. Decide what each one is before you look.

inputs.label: Situations in the set (6 per edition, from src/content/drills/{region}/spot-the-fake.json)
inputs.hint: The lesson's own screens come first, then the bank's. Each new screen is listed with its kind, text, the question's premise, the right answer and the cue its reveal names. The builder writes 2–3 options with a 'why' for each.

defaults.in: The 4 screens from in/protect-your-money/upi-fraud-and-the-clock (refund QR, shop counter QR, 'bank security' code call, 'digital arrest' video call), then 2 new. 'kyc-link': message from 'Unknown number' with lines 'Your bank KYC expires today.' and 'Update now or your account will be blocked: kyc-update.example/verify', action 'Open link'. Q: your account works fine this morning, what do you do? Answer: ignore the link and check through your bank's own app or branch. Cue: a deadline, a threat and a link from an unknown number; a bank does not update KYC through a link in a text. Fake. 'screen-share': call from 'Caller: payments support' with lines 'Your payment of ₹2,000 failed.' and 'Install this screen-sharing app so I can fix it for you.', action 'Install app'. Q: a payment of yours really did fail yesterday. Answer: hang up and raise it in your UPI app's own help section. Cue: a screen-sharing app shows them your PIN and codes. Fake.
defaults.eu: The 3 screens from eu/credit-and-fraud/instant-transfer-check ('new number' friend, close-match landlord, off-platform seller), then 3 new confirm-transfer screens of kind 'request', from 'Your bank app: confirm transfer'. 'changed-iban': amount 520, lines 'To: M. Novak, rent', 'Name check: no match.' and 'The account came in a message: our account has changed.', action 'Send anyway'. Q: the landlord's agent emailed yesterday that the rent account changed. Answer: stop, and confirm with the landlord on a number you already have. Cue: a changed account announced by message, then no match. Fake. 'club-match': amount 45, lines 'To: Riverside Rowing Club', 'Name check: match.' and 'You paid this account in March.', action 'Confirm and send'. Q: the treasurer asked every member for the season fee in person at training. Answer: check the amount, then confirm. Ordinary. 'shop-match': from 'Checkout: instant transfer only', amount 240, lines 'Phone, 60% below other shops.', 'Name check: match. Quickdeal Trading.' and 'Card payment unavailable today.', action 'Confirm and send'. Q: the name check says match. Answer: stop, because a match proves only whose account it is, not that the shop will deliver. Cue: a price far below the market and transfer-only checkout. Fake.

inputs.hint: At least one per set, so refusing everything is not the skill.

defaults.eu: 2 (the close-match landlord and the rowing club)

inputs.label: Reporting route shown at the end (bank field reportTo)

defaults.in: Call 1930 or report at cybercrime.gov.in, the same hour (copied from the UPI lesson)
defaults.eu: Tell your bank first, as soon as you notice, then report it to the police in your country through Europol's reporting page (copied from the instant-transfer lesson)

A closing line: 'Every situation you answered comes back for review in a day or two.'
The reflection line (India: the lesson's own; Europe: 'Which cue would you have missed, and where does it appear in your own bank app?').
The edition's reporting route.
'The lesson behind this', linked.

build.maths: No money arithmetic. The page reads the drill bank src/content/drills/{region}/spot-the-fake.json. The lesson named by fromLesson supplies its drill scenarios first, in order, with checkIds `${lessonId}#d${n}`: the ids the lesson already uses, so no reader reviews one screen twice. The bank's own scenarios follow, with checkIds `${region}/tools/spot-the-fake#${id}`. src/pages/[region]/checks.json.ts emits the bank scenarios with lesson = the tool's edition title and lessonPath = `${region}/tools/spot-the-fake`. edgeCases: JS off: it works, because the forms and CSS reveals are the same as in lessons.
India keeps its slug, its URL and the title 'UPI: spot the fake' (titles.in).

Europe: the reveals explain the name-check rule. A close match shows the name on the account; no match does not.

Switching edition from /in/tools/spot-the-fake to /us lands on the US tools index (regionSub 'tools'), not a 404.
build.whyItHelps: India: ₹805 crore of UPI fraud across 10.64 lakh incidents from April to November 2025 (the India edition's own figure). REGIONAL_TEACHING lists fake-KYC links and screen-sharing apps among the scams to teach. Europe: the EBA-ECB report puts €2.2 billion of 2024's €4.2 billion in fraud losses on credit transfers, with users bearing about 85% (the instant-transfer lesson's source). Verification of payee has been required of euro-area providers since 9 Oct 2025, and REGIONAL_TEACHING lists a verification-of-payee drill as EU format 2. The EU lesson's drill already exists, but it can only be met inside the lesson.
build.modelledOn: SEC HoweyTrade (a realistic fake, then a debrief naming each flag); the Betaalvereniging IBAN-name check outcomes; Bank of America's quiz (a one-line why, neutral feedback). What is different: HTML-first, no real bank or app marks, an ordinary case in every set, no score or comparison, and nothing to type.
risks: Impersonation: MockScreen draws no marks. A unit test denylists real bank, app, platform and regulator names in screen text, and any web address on a screen must end in .example.
Fear framing: at least one ordinary payment per set, and no 'you would have lost €X'.
Teaching the wrong tell: cues are behaviours (a changed account announced by message, a PIN to receive money, a link with a deadline), never interface details a real app might change.

The judges differed. The engineering judge rated the drill-bank work medium, not small, and the content-legal judge asked for a new 'shop' screen kind. Settled by reusing the 'request' kind for the shop (a name-check match teaches the cue better) and dropping the tally script, so no island, inline script or CSP hash is added.

verify.lens: skeptic: safety, scope, content rules and edge cases
problems: The 'kyc-link' cue says 'a bank does not update KYC through a link in a text'. That is an absolute claim, and no cited source makes it. RBI's caution of 2 Feb 2024 describes the pattern (threats to freeze or block, links to unauthorised apps) and says to confirm KYC with the bank directly. It does not say banks never send links. The cue also leans on 'from an unknown number'. A sender is an interface detail that scammers imitate, which breaks the spec's own rule that cues are behaviours and never interface details. A reader could learn that a message which looks like it comes from the bank is safe.

The 'screen-share' cue says a screen-sharing app 'shows them your PIN and codes'. That is technically loose: UPI PIN pads are usually blocked from screen capture. What such apps really do is show your screen and incoming codes, and remote-access apps can control the phone. The spec cites the cybercrime.gov.in brochure as the source for both new India screens. It is a 6 MB image PDF, and I could not extract its text to confirm either cue.

The India set has 1 ordinary screen in 6. A reader who refuses everything is right 5 times in 6, so the rule 'refusing everything is not the skill' is barely tested. It also shows a payment world that is five-sixths scams, which leans toward fear framing. Europe has 2 in 6.

The 'shop-match' screen mixes two apps. The figcaption says 'Payment request' and the sender line says 'Checkout: instant transfer only'. The lines combine shop copy ('Phone, 60% below other shops.', 'Card payment unavailable today.') with the bank's own verification result ('Name check: match.'). No real screen looks like this. More generally, MockScreen labels every 'request' kind 'Payment request', but the EU confirm-transfer screens ('changed-iban', 'club-match', 'shop-match' and the lesson's close-match landlord) are pushes the reader started. The label tells the reader someone asked for the money, which contradicts each premise.

'Quickdeal Trading' is the payee on a screen labelled fake. A web search turns up a real 'QuickDeal' trading product (WADMAX Technologies, for MetaTrader 4) and a 'Quick Deal Company'. Calling a name that collides with real businesses a scam risks both defamation and impersonation, and the planned denylist cannot catch this kind of collision.

MockScreen hard-codes the label for 'call' as 'Incoming video call'. The new 'screen-share' screen is a support phone call ('hang up'), so it gets the wrong label. The lesson's 'bank security team' screen already has the same fault.
'No score is kept' is not true. LessonScript prints 'Correct.' or 'Not quite.' on every reveal and saves the result into the Leitner box in lp:progress.

The fixed closing line, 'Every situation you answered comes back for review in a day or two', is false in four cases. (a) With JavaScript off, which the spec says is supported, nothing is scheduled. (b) With storage blocked or in a private window, nothing persists. (c) A reader who already answered the lesson's screens correctly has them at box 2 or higher, so they come back in 3, 7, 14 or 30 days. (d) Revealing without picking still schedules the screen, although it was not 'answered'.

Scoring the same screen twice in quick succession inflates spacing. The lesson's screens reuse `${lessonId}#d${n}` on the tool page. A reader who does the lesson and then the tool the same day moves each correct screen from box 1 to box 3 (7 days), because the second, immediate recall counts as a spaced retrieval.

There are no constraints on bank ids. (a) A review id over 200 characters makes isProgress fail. loadProgress then returns an empty record and the next save overwrites it, wiping all of the reader's progress. (b) LessonScript treats any check id containing '#q' as a quiz question. A bank id starting with 'q' (e.g. 'qr-refund') would make recordQuiz overwrite the lesson's real quiz result under the page's data-lesson-id. (c) If two scenarios share an id, the later one silently overwrites the other in checks.json.

Amounts can display wrongly. MockScreen calls money() with 0 decimal places, so a non-integer amount (e.g. a €44.50 club fee) shows as €45. The ordinary answer is 'check the amount', so the screen would teach checking a wrong figure. checks.json.ts leaves the amount out of the review `context`, so 'check the amount' cannot be done at review time for 'club-match', 'changed-iban' or 'shop-match'.
The intros hard-code 'Six screens' and 'One is'/'Two are' ordinary. If the lesson's drill gains or loses a scenario, or an `ordinary` flag changes, the intro becomes false and no test catches it.

The new screens carry claims (the KYC rule, the screen-sharing risk, the name-check rule, the transfer-only red flag) but the bank has no `sources` field. The tool page shows sources only through the linked lesson, and the lesson does not cite the KYC or screen-sharing facts. PROJECT_BRIEF principle 7 requires sources.
'KYC' reaches the reader undefined. The tool page has no glossary Terms, although src/content/glossary/kyc.json exists. The content rule says every acronym a reader meets is defined.
The e2e brand denylist covers India names only, and only `.ms-from`/`.ms-action`. It never checks `.ms-line`, where 'To: …' and 'Name check: match. Quickdeal Trading.' sit, and it has no EU names.
The test wording 'any web address must end in .example' fails the spec's own 'kyc-update.example/verify', whose last characters are '/verify'.
Adding `tool: spot-the-fake` to eu/instant-transfer-check changes nothing a reader sees. LessonLayout builds a toolHref only for calculator explorables, so a drill lesson never links to the tool.

Wording and completeness gaps. (a) Per-edition titles ('titles.in') need a ToolMeta field and a resolver, and tools/index.astro prints tool.title, but src/lib/tools.ts is missing from the effort list. (b) The EU intro says 'Six screens at the moment of paying', but two of the six are chats that come before paying. (c) Copying reportTo into the bank duplicates the lesson's field, and the two can drift.

verify.lens: skeptic: facts, rules and sources as of 2026-09-22, plus build correctness against the repo (src/lib/tools.ts, src/pages/[region]/tools/[tool].astro, Drill.astro, MockScreen.astro, LessonScript.astro, checks.json.ts, progress.ts, tests)
problems: India 'kyc-link' cue is wrong: the spec says 'a bank does not update KYC through a link in a text'. RBI does not say that. Its press release of 2 Feb 2024 (prid 57244) says to contact your bank directly and not to click suspicious or unverified links. Its KYC FAQs of 9 Jun 2025 (Q29) only say to use 'utmost caution' with links in KYC SMS or email. Q27 and Q28 say banks must tell customers in advance, send reminders after the due date, and give due notice before closing an account. Some real banks do send re-KYC reminders by SMS, so the tell as written teaches something false.

India 'screen-share' cue is overstated: 'a screen-sharing app shows them your PIN and codes'. RBI's AnyDesk alerts (Feb 2019 and after, as reported) say remote-access apps give the caller control of the phone and let them see OTPs. The PIN part is unsourced. UPI apps usually protect the PIN pad, and RBI's BE(A)WARE PDF sits behind a CAPTCHA and could not be checked. The reveal also misses the checkable fact that makes the premise safe: RBI's TAT circular (DPSS.CO.PD No.629, 20 Sep 2019) says a failed UPI debit is auto-reversed by T+1 at the latest, with ₹100 a day compensation after that.

Stale PIN rule: NPCI OC-226/2025-26 (7 Oct 2025, live from 8 Oct 2025) added optional on-device fingerprint or face approval in place of the UPI PIN, for payments up to ₹5,000. The India cue '(a PIN to receive money)' in the risks and the reused lesson reveals is now incomplete. The ₹1,250 refund-QR screen is under the ₹5,000 limit, so a scam can ask for a fingerprint instead of a PIN.

EU 'changed-iban' screen shows something no bank app can know. The line 'The account came in a message: our account has changed.' sits on a 'Your bank app: confirm transfer' screen, and the bank has no idea where the payer got the IBAN. The screen is also almost identical to the lesson's own opening document: landlord, changed IBAN, no match, 'Send anyway'. It adds little a reader has not already met.

EU 'shop-match' merges two apps on one screen. It has a merchant's checkout ('Checkout: instant transfer only', 'Card payment unavailable today') and the bank's name-check result ('Name check: match. Quickdeal Trading.'). Verification of payee (VoP) runs in the payer's bank app, never on a merchant page. MockScreen also captions every 'request' screen 'Payment request', which is the wrong label for a checkout or a transfer confirmation. In the India edition that same label means a collect request.

'Quickdeal Trading' is close to real businesses: QuickDeal is a real MT4 trading tool from WADMAX, and a Quick Deal Company also trades. Using that name for a fake shop risks pointing at a real firm, and a denylist of banks and apps would not catch it. 'Riverside Rowing Club' is a real club in Adelaide. That is harmless as the ordinary case, but it breaks the invented-names practice the lessons follow (e.g. 'Valtari Property').

Member-state variation is not stated. The ECB's Instant Payments Regulation page says VoP covers both instant and standard euro credit transfers, from 9 Oct 2025 in the euro area only. Providers outside the euro area must receive instant euro transfers from 9 Jan 2027 and send them, with VoP, from 9 Jul 2027. National-currency accounts have their own 2028 date. The EU edition serves readers in Poland, Sweden, Czechia, Hungary, Denmark and Romania, and the tool page never tells them their bank may not show a name check yet.

The India figure in whyItHelps (₹805 crore across 10.64 lakh incidents, April–November 2025) is right: MoS Finance Pankaj Chaudhary gave it in the Lok Sabha on 15 Dec 2025, as IANS and Mint report. But regions.ts cites it only through The420.in, a secondary site. The EU figures check out against the EBA-ECB release of 15 Dec 2025: €4.2bn in 2024, €2.200bn on credit transfers, about 85% borne by users.

The source https://cybercrime.gov.in/pdf/Financial%20Fraud%20Brochures%20final.pdf is a 10-page image-only PDF with no extractable text. Nothing in the spec can be traced to it, and no test or reviewer can check a quote against it.

Check-id collision: LessonScript.astro treats any checkId containing '#q' as a quiz question (poll.dataset.checkId!.includes('#q')). A bank scenario id that starts with 'q' (e.g. 'qr-refund', 'quick-sale') would make in/tools/spot-the-fake#qr-refund count as a quiz item, and recordQuiz would then write a quiz score against the lesson id. The spec's id rule does not stop this.

The closing line 'Every situation you answered comes back for review in a day or two' is false in three cases. progress.schedule() moves a check up one box, and the tool reuses the lesson's checkIds, so a reader who already passed those screens in the lesson gets them back in 3, 7, 14 or 30 days. With JavaScript off nothing is scheduled at all, yet the spec claims the page works with JS off. A reveal with no pick is also scheduled for tomorrow.
The India set is 5 fake to 1 ordinary. Refusing everything scores 5 of 6, which undercuts the spec's own point that 'refusing everything is not the skill'. The EU set has 2 ordinary of 6.

The denylist rule is too narrow. The existing e2e test only checks .ms-from and .ms-action (not .ms-line), only on in/tools/spot-the-fake, and only against Indian names. build.answers: Would I spot a fake job offer before I replied?
build.short: Would I spot a fake job?
build.intro: Made-up job messages, real patterns. Decide what each one is before you look.

build.maths: No money arithmetic. The same drill-bank mechanism as spot-the-fake: the fromLesson's three scenarios keep their ids `${lessonId}#d${n}`, and the bank's scenarios use `${region}/tools/job-offer-check#${id}`, emitted by checks.json.ts with lessonPath `${region}/tools/job-offer-check`. edgeCases: The ordinary jobs are plainly ordinary: met in person, a contract, pay from the employer's own payroll.
The US lesson has three scenarios, not six (content-legal judge), so all three new US screens are written for this bank.
No messaging app, job board or platform is named ('a group chat', 'a big job site'), and every US address ends in .example.
No banned words: proposal 1's 'unlock VIP tasks' is reworded 'move to premium tasks' ('unlock' is on the brand's banned list).
Screens never ask the reader to type anything.
The lesson's three screens keep the lesson's review ids.

Reveals say whose money passes through the account and that moving it can be a crime, without calling the reader a criminal. Details of the law stay in the lessons.
build.whyItHelps: Adults aged 18–59 reported losing money to job scams at more than five times the rate of older adults (FTC data spotlight, Dec 2022). The FTC's 2025 task-scam alert describes small payouts followed by a deposit demanded before any withdrawal. Europol says more than 90% of the mule transactions it identifies are linked to cybercrime, and the EBF names 18–34-year-olds and students as targets. India has shared over 27 lakh mule accounts through its Suspect Registry (Rajya Sabha, 11 March 2026). REGIONAL_TEACHING lists fake part-time job offers for India and a 'don't be a mule' job-ad classifier as EU format 3. Every edition has a job or mule lesson whose drill cannot be reached as a tool.
build.modelledOn: The Europol and EBF #DontBeAMule warning signs as the rubric; the FTC's job-scam, fake-check and task-scam pages; SEC HoweyTrade's fake followed by a debrief. What is different: no name entry, no reward for playing the scammer's side (unlike NGPF's Shady Sam), no game analytics, and two ordinary jobs in every set.
risks: Blame: reveals name the pattern and whose money moves, not the reader.
Impersonation: fictional firms and people only, checked by the denylist test.
Advice: never 'never work online'. The ordinary cases show what real work looks like.
Personal data: nothing is typed.
The judges differed on effort (content-legal: small; engineering: medium, after the drill bank). It is built right after spot-the-fake's bank, which makes it small on its own.
build.effort: small once the drill bank exists: src/lib/tools.ts entry; src/content/drills/in/job-offer-check.json, eu/job-offer-check.json and us/job-offer-check.json (three new scenarios each, with ordinary flags and reportTo); ordinary: true on the lesson screens Sunrise Tutorials, Tutorfeld and Brightline; frontmatter: in/money-mule (spot-the-fake to job-offer-check), eu/money-mule and us/job-scam (add tool: job-offer-check); covered by tests/unit/drills.test.ts. verify.lens: Skeptic: safety and scope (advice, recommendation, named products, promised returns, personal data, moralising, content rules) plus data and edge cases, checked against the repo on branch interactive-tools and the cited FTC, Europol, EBF and IRS pages
problems: UNSAFE ORDINARY CASE (India 'internship-offer'). The spec's answer is 'accept and send the details' in reply to a message that asks for your PAN and bank details before you join and says an offer letter is attached. The reader cannot check who sent a message, and the only cue given is the sender label 'HR, the firm where you interviewed'. Faked offer letters and 'HR' messages that impersonate real employers are a documented pattern: the EBF says mule adverts 'may copy a genuine company's website', and the FTC's 2023 alerts describe fake onboarding portals that collect Social Security and bank numbers. So the drill would teach that sending identity and bank details by message is the safe move. The lesson's own ordinary screen, 'Tutoring centre office: send your account details for salary', already leans the same way, which makes India's two ordinary cases both say 'send details by message'.

BLAME AND ACCURACY IN THE REVEALS. The spec has every reveal say 'whose money would pass through the reader's account' and 'that moving it can be a crime', and the reflection asks 'whose money would have passed through your account?'. In 'premium-tasks', 'joining-kit', 'text-interview' and 'fake-check' the reader is the victim of an advance-fee, identity or fake-check scam, not a mule. Telling someone who paid a ₹1,499 kit fee, or who deposited a fake check, that moving money 'can be a crime' is wrong and puts the blame on them, which the no-moralising rule forbids. In the two ordinary cases no one else's money moves at all.

REVIEW IDS WOULD BE WRONG FOR SITUATIONS 4–6. Drill.astro builds every check id as `${lessonId}#d${index + 1}`, and the tool page passes the lesson's id. So situations 4–6 would be stored as `in/protect-your-money/money-mule#d4..d6`. Those ids do not exist in checks.json, and Review.tsx silently skips unknown ids. The closing line 'Every situation you answered comes back for review' would then be false for half the set. Drill.astro is not in the effort list.

THE DRILL LOOKUP PICKS THE WRONG LESSON IF GENERALISED. [tool].astro hard-codes `tool.slug === 'spot-the-fake'` and finds its lesson with `lessons.find(l => explorable.kind === 'drill' && l.data.reportTo)`, and lessonsFor sorts by `order` only, across tracks. Reused for job-offer-check, that lookup returns in/upi-fraud-and-the-clock (order 1) for India, eu/instant-transfer-check (order 2, ahead of money-mule at order 3) for Europe, and us/paid-promotion (order 3, ahead of job-scam at order 4) for the US: the wrong drill in all three editions. The 'drill bank' and `fromLesson` mechanism the spec relies on does not exist yet: there is no src/content/drills and no drills collection in content.config.ts.

`ordinary: true` WOULD BE DROPPED WITHOUT A WORD. The drill scenario schema is `z.object({ screen, check })` in src/content/schema.ts, and Zod strips unknown keys. The flag on the lesson screens would vanish at parse time, and the '2 of 6 ordinary' test could not see it. `screen` and `check` are also not exported, so a drills test cannot reuse them.

THE CLOSING LINE IS FALSE IN SEVERAL STATES. 'Every situation you answered comes back for review in a day or two' is static text. Nothing is scheduled with JavaScript off (which the spec says is supported) or when localStorage throws in a private window. The lesson's three screens may already sit in Leitner box 3 or higher, so a correct answer moves them to 14 or 30 days, not 'a day or two'.

THE NEW SCREENS FAIL CHECKS THAT DO NOT EXIST YET. The spec says impersonation is 'checked by the denylist test'. The only such test is one e2e assertion on in/tools/spot-the-fake, with an India-only list (RBI, SBI, Paytm, WhatsApp…). Nothing checks EU or US screens, and nothing checks JSON banks. lessons.test.ts covers banned words, market-signal wording, sentence length and undefined acronyms for lessons only, and tests/unit/drills.test.ts does not exist. 'Kovač Bakery' uses a very common Central European surname and could match a real bakery. 'Brightline' (the US lesson's ordinary advert) is a real US brand name.

UNDEFINED ACRONYMS ON A PAGE WITH NO GLOSSARY. The screens and reveals use PAN, TDS (India), IBAN (EU), SSN and Form I-9 (US). The tool page renders no Term popovers, and CONTENT_GUIDE requires every acronym a reader meets to be defined. The glossary has no 'ssn' entry.

THE SCREEN FRAME CONTRADICTS THE CUES. MockScreen renders kind 'message' with the caption 'Text message'. 'payment-agent' makes its cue '(a free email address)', and 'internship-offer' and 'apprenticeship' say a document is 'attached'. A text message has no email address and no attachments, so the tell the reader is meant to spot contradicts the frame around it.

THE US 'fake-check' PREMISE CONTRADICTS ITS BUTTON. The question says the check already shows in your app, which means it was deposited, but the action button is 'Deposit and send'. In 'text-interview', 'an employer collects your SSN on forms after an offer' does not tell the real employer from the scam: the FTC documents fake 'onboarding' forms that collect exactly that. The dependable tells are being hired by text with no call, and the request for a banking login.

THE TOOL'S TYPE IS AMBIGUOUS AND GETS MISLABELLED. ToolMeta has no kind field. [tool].astro keys the 'Practice' label and the header regionSub off `tool.regions`, and the home page lists `TOOLS.filter(t => !t.regions)` under 'Calculators that answer'. With editions ['in','eu','us'], a builder who omits `regions` ('omitted means all') gets a drill labelled 'Calculator' and listed on the home page as a calculator. Its footer would then say 'The numbers it opens with are an example', and the edition front would say 'Change any of them to match your own'. The tools index lede says 'and a practice drill' (singular), and India would have two.

THE LESSONS WOULD STILL NOT LINK TO THE DRILL. LessonLayout builds toolHref only for the margin, split, loan and growth explorers. A drill lesson renders no link to any tool, so adding `tool: job-offer-check` to eu/money-mule and us/job-scam changes nothing a reader sees. `tool` is also an unchecked z.string(), so a typo passes.

THE SPEC DOES NOT MATCH THE REPO. The India lesson's ordinary screen is 'Tutoring centre office', not 'Sunrise Tutorials', so 'ordinary: true on … Sunrise Tutorials' matches nothing. The EU reportTo text differs from the lesson's label, and copying it into JSON will drift. The Poll options and their 'why' lines, which are what the reader actually sees, are left to the builder and so escape this review.

THE ANSWER PATTERN CAN BE GAMED. In every edition the ordinary cases sit at positions 2 and 6, in a fixed order, and the intro announces 'Two are ordinary'. Once two ordinary screens are found, the rest can be deduced rather than judged.

DATA EDGE CASES ARE NOT HANDLED. (a) If the bank file or the fromLesson is missing, or the lesson loses its drill, the page must not build, and the index filters (`tool.slug !== 'spot-the-fake' || hasDrill`) would still link job-offer-check, giving a 404. (b) Duplicate scenario ids, an answer index out of range, or an empty bank are unguarded outside the lesson schema. (c) LessonScript treats any check id containing '#q' as a quiz item, so a future bank id such as 'qr-offer' would be scored as a lesson quiz.
